papers.title: MEWAC – Collaborative Project EXALT: Coupling thermal desalination and extraction of dewatered salt with hydroponic greenhouse cultivtion via heat pumps - Middle East Regional Water Research Cooperation Program (MEWAC)
papers.title_normalized: mewac collaborative project exalt coupling thermal desalination and extraction of dewatered salt with hydroponic greenhouse cultivtion via heat pumps middle east regional water research cooperation program mewac
papers.authors: Jörn Germer; Alexander Morgenstern; Yana Abu Taleb; Moshe Shenker
papers.abstract: The EXALT project, supported by the MEWAC funding initiative, aimed to deliver practical solutions to water scarcity in the Middle East through trinational collaboration between German, Jordanian, and Israeli partners (Figure 1). Crop production in the region is constrained by chronic water scarcity, exacerbated by climate change, recurrent droughts, and salinization of freshwater and soils. In the Jordan River Basin, per capita renewable water availability has declined by more than 80% over six decades, while agriculture remains the largest consumer of water, using roughly half of total freshwater withdrawals in both Jordan and Israel. The two countries pursue divergent strategies to address water scarcity: Jordan depends on declining groundwater and transboundary surface water, supplemented by limited freshwater imports from Israel, whereas Israel relies heavily on large-scale desalination and direct wastewater reuse. In this context, EXALT developed a blueprint for innovative hydroponic greenhouse systems to overcome both water scarcity and salinity constraints. By combining advanced climate control, water recovery, and thermal desalination, the project sought to maximize water-use efficiency, reduce environmental pressures, enhance year-round productivity, and provide a scalable model for arid, subtropical regions. From the outset, the consortium emphasized integrated collaboration across technical, scientific, and capacity-building dimensions, including controlled-environment trials, field assessments, stakeholder engagement, and training of young scientists. EcoPeace Jordan supported these efforts by organizing field trips for researchers, conducting interviews, and assisting with soil sampling campaigns, while a number of universities and public institutions contributed local knowledge, sample analysis, and networking support. Research at the University of Hohenheim examined the interplay of atmospheric demand, salinity, and plant performance in hydroponic systems. Three experiments with tomato, cucumber, and quinoa demonstrated genotype-specific responses in growth, ion partitioning, and stress tolerance. Salt-tolerant tomatoes effectively sequestered sodium and chloride in the petiole, protecting metabolically active leaf tissues, while cucumbers showed lower ionic homeostasis and increased vulnerability under high vapour pressure deficit (VPD). Evapotranspiration was strongly influenced by both VPD and light regime, with LED lighting reducing water loss relative to metal halide lamps. These findings underscore the importance of coordinating humidity, light, and salinity management to optimize plant performance and water-use efficiency. At the University of Jerusalem, experiments compared nutrient uptake in recirculating deep-water culture and nutrient film technique systems. Leaf nutrient concentrations generally reflected solution composition, yet NFT systems maintained optimal nutrient levels even when solution concentrations exceeded targets. Preliminary studies on chelate dynamics suggested interactions that could limit micronutrient availability, highlighting the importance of nutrient management under low-input and saline conditions. Fraunhofer research focused on greenhouse energy efficiency and climate control (Figure 2). Thermal screens improved heat retention, LED lighting reduced electrical demand, and partial photovoltaic shading lowered heat gain while allowing recovery of water from condensation. Simulation studies of a fully controlled growing environment (FCGE) indicated potential for year-round cultivation, wastewater elimination, and substantial reduction of external water requirements. FCGE systems demonstrated high yields, significant water savings, and resilience under semi-arid and saline conditions. Collectively, the consortium showed that hydroponic systems with integrated climate and water-recovery technologies could reduce daily water demand by up to 2.25 L m⁻², nearly matching the annual irrigation allocation for protected vegetables in the Jordan Valley. Applied across an estimated 4,000 ha of greenhouse cultivation, these technologies could save roughly 19–22 million m³ of water annually - about 17% of the total supply from the King Abdullah Canal and equivalent to the freshwater needs of several hundred thousand people. At the same time, crop- and genotype-specific salt uptake was shown to enable biological removal of salts through harvested biomass, reducing or eliminating the need for energy-intensive brine management under moderate salinity conditions. Together, these findings demonstrate that closed-loop hydroponic systems can simultaneously address water scarcity and salinity constraints while substantially lowering energy demand and operational costs. Despite geopolitical tensions limiting in-region mobility and field activities, the consortium maintained continuous communication, shared methodologies, and harmonized workflows, reflecting a common understanding of regional water and agricultural challenges. Capacity-building activities included MSc, BSc, and doctoral-level research projects, remote mentoring, and cross-institutional supervision. These efforts strengthened human capital across Israel, Jordan, and Germany, creating a cadre of trained professionals ready to implement water-efficient agricultural technologies and support future science–industry collaboration. Through technical innovation, environmental monitoring, and capacity development, EXALT advanced sustainable greenhouse production, disseminated environmentally innovative technologies, and fostered long-term professional networks. By addressing both water scarcity and salinity, the project contributes to regional water security, demonstrates the value of cross-border cooperation, and provides a replicable model for sustainable agriculture under challenging conditions. Even under restricted mobility and political constraints, the consortium’s integrated approach delivered measurable contributions to technology transfer, capacity building, and resilient agricultural practices.

papers.title: Water as an argument for peace and cooperation in transboundary basins
papers.title_normalized: water as an argument for peace and cooperation in transboundary basins
papers.abstract: When talking about the human rights to safe drinking water and sanitation, I often pause to reflect, thinking about our own families, on what the lack of safe drinking water at home can mean; to reflect on the suffering, the daily insecurity and the exhausting work that it is, in fact, for so many women and girls to fetch the water they need at home every day… Of the well over 2 billion people who are not guaranteed the human right to safe drinking water, many live in the 153 countries that share river basins and aquatic ecosystems. In these countries, each state's obligation to ensure the human rights to safe drinking water and sanitation within its borders inexorably becomes a shared responsibility at the basin level. On the other hand, in the face of the growing risks of droughts and floods generated by climate change, we must understand that, just as storms and hurricanes do not recognize spaces of national sovereignty, rivers do not recognize borders when it comes to droughts and floods. Droughts and floods not only jeopardize access to drinking water and sanitation for hundreds of millions of people but also to food and health, causing increasing processes of mass migration, violence, and social and political destabilization in entire regions. The traditional approach to water management as a simple economic resource at the national level encourages competition and conflict between neighboring peoples, making it difficult to cope with the risks of climate change. Couple this resource approach with the manipulation of national sovereignty arguments over the waters that flow through each country and the risk of armed conflict skyrockets. At times, the logic of hatred that presides over armed conflicts is also leading to the use of water as a weapon of war against the civilian population, resulting in crimes that can be qualified as genocide insofar as they threaten the lives of millions of civilians, as is happening in Gaza. The international community cannot allow this to happen. We need to develop new ecosystem approaches, based on human rights, at the basin scale. Such approaches allow us to move from competition for resources to shared responsibility for the sustainable management of ecosystems and climate change risks for the benefit of all, ensuring the human rights and basic needs of all basin dwellers. This is not only an ethical and justice requirement but a global necessity if we are to address climate change and promote peace, security, and survival for hundreds of millions of people. A human rights-based approach must also promote cross-border public participation, particularly of those living in the greatest vulnerability, and with special attention to the effective participation of women. Adopting an ecosystem approach that prioritizes human rights will not in itself solve conflicts and wars, where water is often used as a confrontational argument, but it can prevent conflicts, open prospects for solutions, and build peace and cooperation in post-conflict situations. Building trust and hope by ensuring water security is a good basis for building peace and security among those who share rivers and aquifers. In the perspective of ongoing climate change, it is urgent that states sharing transboundary basins sign the UN Water Convention and promote transboundary agreements and institutions that allow them to develop shared responsibility for the management of their basins. Furthermore, the Security Council should pay attention to transboundary water management as a key to peace and security, in line with the Swiss and Slovenian proposals and the recommendations of the Peacebuilding Commission. It is worth highlighting the global leadership offered by the African continent in the development of the management principles and criteria promoted by the UN Water Convention, with transboundary agreements and institutions in the basins of Lake Chad and the Senegal, Niger, and Okavango rivers, among others, making explicit priority commitments to guarantee the human right to drinking water and the basic needs of the populations, as well as transboundary public and community participation. In Europe, the EU Framework Directive also offers a reference example in the development of the shared responsibility of States in transboundary basins to restore and maintain the good ecological status of ecosystems, beyond the quality and potability of supplies. The Albufeira Convention provides an example of this. However, nothing is committed, either in the Water Framework Directive or in conventions such as the Albufeira Convention, in terms of human rights or transboundary public participation. WWP – 2024 – 112 *Translation into Spanish* Título: El agua como argumento de paz y cooperación en cuencas transfronterizas. Autor: Pedro Arrojo Agudo. 1 Afiliación: Profesor de análisis económico en la Universdiad de Zaragoza (España). Contacto: [email protected] Palabras clave: derechos humanos, paz, conflictos, cuencas transfronterizas, gestión del agua Cuando hablo de los derechos humanos al agua potable y al saneamiento, a menudo me detengo a reflexionar, pensando en nuestras propias familias, sobre lo que puede significar la falta de agua potable en el hogar; a reflexionar sobre el sufrimiento, la inseguridad diaria y el trabajo agotador que supone, de hecho, para tantas mujeres y niñas ir a buscar el agua que necesitan en casa todos los días… De los más de 2.000 millones de personas a quienes no se les garantiza el derecho humano al agua potable, muchas viven en los 153 países que comparten cuencas fluviales y ecosistemas acuáticos. En esos países, la obligación de cada Estado de garantizar el derecho humano al agua potable y al saneamiento dentro de sus fronteras se convierte inexorablemente en una responsabilidad compartida a nivel de cuenca. Por otro lado, frente a los crecientes riesgos de sequías e inundaciones generados por el cambio climático, debemos comprender que, así como las tormentas y los huracanes no reconocen espacios de soberanía nacional, los ríos no reconocen fronteras cuando se trata de sequías e inundaciones. Las sequías e inundaciones no sólo ponen en peligro el acceso al agua potable y al saneamiento de cientos de millones de personas, sino también a la alimentación y la salud, provocando crecientes procesos de migración masiva, violencia y desestabilización social y política en regiones enteras. El enfoque tradicional de la gestión del agua como un simple recurso económico a nivel nacional fomenta la competencia y los conflictos entre pueblos vecinos, lo que dificulta hacer frente a los riesgos del cambio climático. Si a este enfoque de los recursos se suma la manipulación de los argumentos de soberanía nacional sobre las aguas que fluyen por cada país, el riesgo de conflicto armado se dispara. En ocasiones, la lógica del odio que preside los conflictos armados también lleva a utilizar el agua como arma de guerra contra la población civil, dando lugar a crímenes que pueden calificarse de genocidio en la medida en que amenazan la vida de millones de civiles, como está sucediendo en Gaza. La comunidad internacional no puede permitir que esto ocurra. Necesitamos desarrollar nuevos enfoques ecosistémicos, basados en los derechos humanos, a escala de cuenca. Estos enfoques nos permiten pasar de la competencia por los recursos a la responsabilidad compartida por la gestión sostenible de los ecosistemas y los riesgos del cambio climático en beneficio de todos, garantizando los derechos humanos y las necesidades básicas de todos los habitantes de la cuenca. No se trata sólo de un requisito ético y de justicia, sino de una necesidad global si queremos abordar el cambio climático y promover la paz, la seguridad y la supervivencia de cientos de millones de personas. Un enfoque basado en los derechos humanos también debe promover la participación pública transfronteriza, en particular de quienes viven en mayor vulnerabilidad, y con especial atención a la participación efectiva de las mujeres. La adopción de un enfoque ecosistémico que dé prioridad a los derechos humanos no resolverá por sí sola los conflictos y las guerras, en los que el agua suele utilizarse como argumento de confrontación, pero puede prevenir conflictos, abrir perspectivas de soluciones y generar paz y cooperación en situaciones posteriores a conflictos. Generar confianza y esperanza garantizando la seguridad hídrica es una buena base para generar paz y seguridad entre quienes comparten ríos y acuíferos. Ante el cambio climático en curso, es urgente que los Estados que comparten cuencas transfronterizas firmen la Convención de las Naciones Unidas sobre el Agua y promuevan acuerdos e instituciones transfronterizas que les permitan desarrollar una responsabilidad compartida en la gestión de sus cuencas. Además, el Consejo de Seguridad debería prestar atención a la gestión de las aguas transfronterizas como clave para la paz y la seguridad, de acuerdo con las propuestas suizas y eslovenas y las recomendaciones de la Comisión de Consolidación de la Paz. Cabe destacar el liderazgo global que ofrece el continente africano en el desarrollo de los principios y criterios de gestión que promueve la Convención de la ONU sobre el Agua, con acuerdos e instituciones transfronterizas en las cuencas del lago Chad y de los ríos Senegal, Níger y Okavango, entre otros, asumiendo compromisos prioritarios explícitos para garantizar el derecho humano al agua potable y las necesidades básicas de las poblaciones, así como la participación pública y comunitaria transfronteriza. En Europa, la Directiva Marco de la UE también ofrece un ejemplo de referencia en el desarrollo de la responsabilidad compartida de los Estados en las cuencas transfronterizas para restablecer y mantener el buen estado ecológico de los ecosistemas, más allá de la calidad y la potabilidad de los suministros. El Convenio de Albufeira es un ejemplo de ello. Sin embargo, ni en la Directiva Marco del Agua ni en convenios como el Convenio de Albufeira se compromete nada en materia de derechos humanos o de participación pública transfronteriza. WWP-2024-112. *Chinese Translation*. 标题:水作为跨边界流域和平与合作的论据. Author: Pedro Arrojo Agudo.2 Affiliation: Professor of Economic Analysis at the University of Zaragoza (Spain). Contact: [email protected] 关键词 人权, 和平, 冲突, 跨边界流域, 水管理 当谈到安全饮用水和卫生设施方面的人权时, 我经常停下来反思我们的家庭, 思考家里缺乏安全饮用水可能意味着什么；反思这么多妇女和女孩每天取水 (供家庭使用)所面临的痛苦、日常的不安全感和疲惫不堪的工作 … … 超过20亿人的安全饮用水权得不到保障, 其中许多人生活在共享河流流域和水生生态系统的153个国家。在这些国家中, 每个国家在“确保其境内安全饮用水和卫生设施人权”方面的义务不可避免地成为流域层面的共同责任。. 另一方面, 面对气候变化带来的日益严重的干旱和洪水风险, 我们必须认识到, 正如风暴和飓风不承认国家主权空间一样, 河流在干旱和洪水问题上也不承认边界。干旱和洪水不仅危及数亿人获得饮用水和卫生设施, 而且危及粮食和健康, 导致整个地区大规模移民、暴力以及社会和政治不稳定的进程不断加剧。. 传统的水管理方式作为国家层面的简单经济资源, 鼓励了邻近民族之间的竞争和冲突, 使得“应对气候变化风险”一事变得困难。将这种资源方法与操纵国家主权争议 (关于流经各国的水域)相结合, 武装冲突的风险就会飙升。. 有时, 主导武装冲突的仇恨逻辑也导致水被作为针对平民的战争武器, 造成可被定性为种族灭绝的罪行, 因为它们威胁到数百万平民的生命, 就像加沙正在发生的那样。国际社会不能允许这种情况发生。. 我们需要在流域范围内制定基于人权的新生态系统方法。这些方法使我们能够从资源竞争转向共同承担可持续生态系统管理责任和气候变化风险, 以造福所有人, 同时保障所有流域居民的人权和基本需求。. 如果我们要应对气候变化并促进亿万人民的和平、安全和生存, 这就不仅是伦理和正义的要求, 也是全球的必然要求。. 基于人权的方法还必须促进跨边界公众参与, 特别是那些最脆弱群体的公众参与, 并特别关注妇女的有效参与。. 采用优先考虑人权的生态系统方法本身并不能解决冲突和战争, 因为水经常被用作对抗性论据, 但它可以预防冲突, 开辟解决方案的前景, 并在冲突后局势中建立和平与合作。通过确保水安全以建立信任和希望, 为“在共享河流和含水层的人们之间建立和平与安全”提供了良好基础。. 鉴于持续的气候变化, 共享跨边界流域的国家应尽快签署《联合国水公约》, 并推动建立跨边界协议和机构, 使各国能够共同承担流域管理的责任。. 此外, 联合国安理会应关注跨边界水管理, 将其作为和平与安全的关键, 这符合瑞士和斯洛文尼亚的提议以及建设和平委员会的建议。. 值得强调的是, 非洲大陆在制定《联合国水公约》所倡导的管理原则和标准方面发挥了全球领导作用, 乍得湖、塞内加尔河、尼日尔河和奥卡万戈河等流域的跨边界协议和机构明确承诺优先保障人民的饮用水权利和基本需求, 以及跨边界公众和社区的参与。. 在欧洲, 《欧盟水框架指令》也为各国在跨边界流域共同承担责任提供了一个参考范例, 这一责任在于恢复和维护生态系统的良好生态状态, 而不仅仅是水源的质量和可饮用性。《阿尔布费拉公约》就是一个例子。然而, 无论是《水框架指令》还是《阿尔布费拉公约》等, 都没有在人权或跨边界公众参与方面作出任何承诺。.

papers.title: Waste and Discard in Italy and the Mediterranean: Theories, Practices, Literature and Film
papers.title_normalized: waste and discard in italy and the mediterranean theories practices literature and film
papers.abstract: If we were to trace the development of the field of waste studies in Italy, we might note the importance, though seldom acknowledged, of Danilo Dolci's Spreco (1960), an examination of the nexus of poverty, resource mismanagement, environmental degradation, and organized crime in western Sicily in the mid-twentieth century. While fighting for the equitable management of natural resources, along with improved sewage and other infrastructure for Sicily's poorest communities, Dolci established the connection between these problems and the waste of discarded individuals, communities and their potential, a connection that has become fundamental to many contributions to waste studies. The most recent of these, Waste and Discard in Italy and the Mediterranean: Theories, Practices, Literature and Film, edited by Damiano Benvegnù, Marta Cariello, Matteo Gilebbi and Graziella Parati, similarly reaffirms the semantic reach of “waste” to address both material and socioecological realities, with an emphasis on resulting social disparities and exclusions.As the title suggests, the essays in the collection are divided into four sections, together with an introduction by the editors and an afterword by Gabriele Geminiani, founder of MICRO, the Museum of the Rediscovered Objects, who offers as a counterpoint to the rest of the volume the beauty and value of discarded objects put on display, prompting visitor-consumers to consider their own role in this ecosystem. The first pair of essays (“Theories”), Pasquale Verdicchio's “Migration, Environment, Representation: A ‘Sea Change into Something Rich and Strange’” and Graziella Parati's “Flotsam: Bodies, Trash, and Mediterranean Migrations,” critique the rhetoric of waste as applied to migrant bodies in the Mediterranean and raise possibilities for new dispositions that acknowledge the interconnectedness of human and nonhuman, visible and invisible, public and private, and North and South. Parati makes a compelling case for one of these dispositions, an “ethics of care,” as developed in the context of Italian feminist philosophy.The authors included in the following section (“Practices”) examine spaces where human action has led to intractable problems involving toxicity and the remediation and reclamation of ruined landscapes. Rebecca Falkoff follows the process, beset with political and commercial interests, of relocating the Piazza dei Ciompi market in Florence (“We'll Always Have Florence: Asbestos, Abatement, and Obsolete Objects at the Piazza dei Ciompi Market”). Sophia Maxine Farmer explores and proposes solutions to the enduring presence of controversial monuments to Italy's Fascist past (“Conserving Fascism's Legacy: The Politics of Waste, Preservation, and Erasure”). In Dylan Gilbert's “Polluted Lands, Poisoned Futures: A Trans-Corporeal Case Study of Scanzano Jonico's Antinuclear Protests,” resistance to the creation of a nuclear waste depository in Basilicata underscores the transcorporeal connection between the health of the land and that of its human residents.Five essays (“Literature”) read literary works to explore the relationship between human vulnerability and the power of waste throughout the Mediterranean. Carmine Di Biase examines how the anthropomorphization of trash in Alessandro Casola's play ’A Munnezza serves to resist “the illusion of a purely human, anthropocentric society” (139). In “Carlotto's Perdas de Fogu: Toxicity and National Security in the Mediterranean Basin,” Anna Chiafele reads Carlotto's noir novel as an “intricate story of violence, power, and socioecological injustice” that unmasks the threat to human and nonhuman bodies near a military testing ground located in Sardinia (145). Simonetta Falasca-Zamponi discusses Roberto Saviano's Gomorrah as an extreme example of capitalism's reliance on the disposability of all elements of an ecosystem, both human and nonhuman (“On the Logic of Disposability: Gomorrah's Invisible Risks”). Martino Lovato focuses on postmodern elements and the “claim to truth” in Egyptian novelist Sonallah Ibrahim's Dhat, as a way of critiquing the role of the state and the uneasy process of globalization over several decades (“Trash as a Marker of the Third-World Condition in Sonallah Ibrahim's Dhat”). In “‘A Washed Pig Returns to the Mud’: The Working-Class in Greek Literature in the Interwar Years and the 1980s,” Vasiliki Petsa demonstrates how literary representations of the working-class appeal to a politically motivated iconography of dirt, pollution and decay as cultural markers of social ills.Two essays (“Film”) read cinematic depictions of Southern Italian spaces where the notion of waste characterizes both marginalized human lives and the environments they inhabit. Laura Di Bianco's “Currents in Italian Cinema of the Wasteocene: The Vice of Hope by Edoardo De Angelis” takes an ecocritical approach to a “dystopian melodrama about women and infants trafficked among the banks of a river, the Volturno, amidst its detritus” (234). In Ilaria Puliti's “Aesthetics of Toxicity: Disposable Ships and Car Wrecks in Frammartino's Il dono,” the film provides a counternarrative to conventional depictions of the Calabrian south, focusing instead on visualizing the “storied matter” of waste and toxicity. Both essays illustrate the exceptional power of cinema to shift perspectives away from anthropocentric narratives and foster a disposition of care.Waste and Discard in Italy and the Mediterranean offers a number of stories of the Wasteocene with broad political, social, and aesthetic implications for readers interested in understanding and resisting the destruction of environments and communities in Italy and beyond. Indeed, as we have come to expect of scholarship in the environmental humanities, these essays help us realign our experiences and gain a more sustainable and just relationship between ourselves and the nonhuman world. The collection is well curated, with an insightful introduction and a brief preface to each of the four sections, situating the essays in relation to key contributions in waste studies, new materialism, and ecocriticism. Moreover, we might agree with Marco Armiero that the Mediterranean could stand as “the epitome of the Wasteocene, the conceptual and material border against which thousands of humans crash in their attempt to force the boundaries dividing those who value and those who are disposable” (5). However, because the authors often take care to place their studies of Mediterranean texts into a broader global context, Waste and Discard will be of considerable interest to scholars whose work addresses other contexts around the globe.

papers.title: Editor's Introduction
papers.title_normalized: editor s introduction
papers.abstract: This issue includes ten articles that are grouped by four themes. The first group, which consists of Kevin Michael Smith's “The Promise of (Un)happiness: 34 Literature and Yi Si-u's Surrealist Poetics in Colonial Korea,” Ferran de Vargas's “Japanese New Left's Political Theories of Subjectivity and Ōshima Nagisa's Practice of Cinema,” So-Rim Lee's “Between Plastic Surgery and the Photographic Representation: Ji Yeo Undoes the Elusive Narrative of Transformation,” and Andrew Campana's “You Forbid Me to Walk: Yokota Hiroshi's Disability Poetics,” addresses the question of subjectivation. Kevin Michael Smith examines a literary surrealist movement in colonial Korea by exploring the dialectics of the colonial regime of (un)happiness and poetic forms of seeking utopian shards of freedom. Taking a psychoanalytic approach to Yi Si-u's poetry published in 34 Literature, Smith proposes a new interpretation of Korean surrealism as a dialectical engagement with the colonial system of interpellation, a system that produced “happiness” as an affective system of control and oppression. Smith argues that Yi's poetry brought to the fore (un)happiness or “dark” aspects of human psychology such as trauma, sadness, tragedy, and death drive that belonged to the everyday realm of unconsciousness. Yi's poetic trope disclosed, according to Smith, utopian shards of happiness and liberation precisely because of its engagement with the unconscious world of despair and depression under colonial rule. Following Herbert Marcuse's observation that individual happiness and freedom can be compatible with the preservation of common existence only when egalitarian organizational forms guarantee material subsistence and human reproduction, Smith concludes that Yi's poetry speaks to the truism that individual gratification is predicated on the guarantee of collective well-being.If Smith explores how the surrealist's articulation of a state of abjection worked as a condition of possibility for the dialectics of subjectivation in colonial Korea, Ferran de Vargas introduces the Japanese New Left's theories of the dialectics of subjectivation in their deployment of the concept of nothingness (mu) or self-negation (jikohitei). De Vargas situates the film director Ōshima Nagisa's Kōshukei, which was based on the 1958 Komatsugawa Incident, within a broader New Left discourse that privileged self-negation (i.e., bourgeois self) as the onto-epistemological ground for individual autonomy or as a state of pure subjectivity that generated a drive to subvert the system of modern (capitalist) alienation. Despite their differences, according to De Vargas, leading New Left theorists such as Umemoto Katsumi, Nakai Masakazu, Yoshimoto Takaaki, Tanigawa Gan, and Tokoto Mitsuko all embraced the theory of subjective nothingness. Ōshima's Kōshukei drew inspiration from Umemoto's theory, as well as existential philosophy such as Sartreanism, for its portrayal of the protagonist R, who in the film develops a rebel subjectivity as a result of “the experience of alienation, of the denial of control over his own being by external social powers.” De Vargas concludes that it is crucial to understand Ōshima's cinematic practice in the context of the Japanese New Left's theories, which offered a far less deterministic view of subjectivation rooted in subjectivism of nothingness, a nondeterministic dialectic of the subjective and the objective, than the well-known Marxian theory of subjectivation developed by Louis Althusser.So-Rim Lee's “Between Plastic Surgery and the Photographic Representation” shifts our attention to the neoliberal fantasy of the desirable subject. Lee focuses on New York–based South Korean photographer Ji Yeo's photographic series Beauty Recovery Room and It Will Hurt a Little to probe how photographic representation of plastic surgery reveals and demystifies the illusive narrative of beautification and upward mobility promised by South Korea's plastic surgery industry. Lee demonstrates how Yeo's photographic images underscore surgery not as a process of obtaining substantive transformation or aspirational personhood that are conducive to the norms of desirability under the neoliberal order, but as a practice of bodily rupture that involves an affective, material, and durational process of painful recovery. The plastic surgery industry's marketing strategy of promoting the fantasy of empowerment is a mode of subject-formation putatively capable of helping patients attain social recognition in the competitive and surface-image-driven world. Lee shows how plastic surgery embodies and draws from the logic of neoliberal ideology through its interpellation of the body into social capital. It was no coincidence, according to Lee, that the 1994 financial crisis that led to the installation of a neoliberal economy in South Korea marked a turning point for the ascendance of the plastic surgery industry. Lee concludes that Yeo's images of bodily rupture refuse any simple narrativization of surgical experience and work as antinarrative to the neoliberal logic of upward mobility by humanizing individual patients in their revelation of the solitary process of recovery.Andrew Campana's “You Forbid Me to Walk” addresses the body “disabled” and stigmatized by cerebral palsy. Campana focuses on the poet Yokota Hiroshi, a leader in Japan's disability rights movement, and the way he used his experiences of having cerebral palsy to create a new kind of “disability” poetics. According to Campana, Yokota's poetic form shows consistent resistance against the normalization of “able” bodies or the “givenness” of the body by provoking a perspective that demonstrates how social forces such as policy discourse, spatial arrangement, and infrastructures disable a certain kind of corporeal existence. Campana argues that Yokota's use of a “body otherwise” challenges “conventional conceptions of what it means to be disabled, as well as what it means to have and be a body.” The body otherwise, writing otherwise, and speaking otherwise in Yokota's performance and poetics radically problematizes the cognitive and material conditions that produce and naturalize the distinction between the “abled” and “disabled” bodies. Yokota's work requires, Campana concludes, its readers and audiences to adapt to a different mode of understanding, sensation, and relating to others, defamiliarizing and decentering the normative mode of social relations and interactions that privilege the “able” body. In this sense, Yokota's work is an example par excellence of resistance against the regime of interpellation in its radical questioning of received norms and practices, senses and sensations, both personal and institutional.The second group takes up the question of memory. Olga Fedorenko's “The Advertising Museum in Seoul: Dream-Images and the Freedom to Advertise” carries out a Benjaminian analysis of the Advertising Museum in Seoul. Building on the scholarship on collective dreamworlds and on advertisement as dream-images, Fedorenko not only teases out how the historicist underpinnings of the museum construct the post-democratization South Korean present as a triumphant moment of technological, political, and aesthetic freedom but also discusses how the dream-images of the old advertisements inadvertently conjure unrealized collective utopias sedimented within them. According to Fedorenko, the pastness of pre-democratization advertisements is brought into the present in such a way as to support the progressive narrative of history and to legitimize post-democratization South Korea as a terminus whereby major historical tasks (i.e., establishment of procedural democracy and institutionalization of liberal freedoms) have been accomplished. This fantasy of arrival fulfills the ideological function of generating dream scenes of South Korea's progress, prosperity, and prestige while trivializing persisting economic and social injustices caused by neoliberal capitalism as merely minor wrinkles. Such fantasies affirm, Fedorenko argues, the dominant official discourse that there are no better alternatives than the catastrophes of the neoliberal present. These advertisements, however, possess dialectical potentialities of redeeming collective dreams of egalitarian democracy and confronting the failure of their realization. In this sense, Fedorenko insists, advertising should be understood as a repository of “unfulfilled pasts, whose will-have-beens unlock hereafters discontinuous from the now.”Chialan Sharon Wang's “Native Soil of Postmemory and Affective Archives in Wu Ming-Yi's The Stolen Bicycle” examines “postmemory” as a significant dimension of Taiwan's cultural memory that offers a counternarrative to totalizing official history. Postmemory refers to, Wang explains, “the relationship that the ‘generation after’ bears to the personal, collective, and cultural trauma of those who came before” (Hirsch 2012: 5) and “unpacks the cross-generational transference of traumatic experiences both within and across species.” By reading Wu's The Stolen Bicycle as a nativist work that reveals memory as a multidirectional and multigenerational construct, Wang teases out how threads of personal memory present multifarious accounts or polyphony of colonialism, wars, and the White Terror. In Wu's works, according to Wang, multidirectional and multigenerational postmemories not only (re)construct human events but also offer a vision of symbiotic community in which humans and nonhumans are engaged in complex relationships deeply entangled with historical violence such as war and genocide. Such post-anthropocentric memories are a product of imaginative investment, projection, and creation that occur in the cross-generational transference of traumatic experiences. They are profoundly local and personal, and constitute an “archive of feelings,” challenging common understandings of what makes an archive.The third group addresses the question of border and identity. Eun Ah Cho's “Familiar Strangers: North Koreans as ‘Dangerous Refugees’ and the Crisis of Korean Chinese Community in Zhang Lu's Dooman River (2010)” examines how two types of border crossing—the crossing of North Koreans into China and the crossing of Korean Chinese into South Korea—cause a crisis of community in a way that confronts the questions of collective ethics and responsibility to others. Cho focuses on a Korean Chinese boy (Chang-ho) in the film Dooman River as a figure symbolizing refugees who have no choice but to take their captivity or nonhome as a home in which to live a precarious life. Chang-ho takes his own life to demand the release of his North Korean friend (Jung-jin) who frequently crosses the border to find some food for his sick sister. The captivity of Jung-jin signifies, according to Cho, the Korean Chinese villagers’ disavowal of shared identity and ethical obligations they felt toward the North Koreans, announcing the insurmountable legal and emotional boundary to the latter. For the Korean Chinese, the North Koreans are after all “familiar strangers.” Cho interprets Chang-ho's death as a sacrifice suggested to audiences by the director of Dooman River in an attempt to preserve the communitarian ethics of Korean Chinese and maintain the value of ethnic identity.Yi-Ting Chang's “Archipelagic Optics in Wu Ming-Yi's The Man with the Compound Eyes” calls for a fundamental rethinking of the epistemological framework of transpacific and Asian/American studies by shifting our inquiries from an intercontinental and nation-state–centered perspective to “archipelagic optics” that foreground “noninnocent multiplicity, decontinental seeing, and immanent dependencies.” Seen from archipelagic optics, Chang argues, boundaries determined by the global system of sovereignty and nation-states lose their onto-political meanings and give way to forms and relations of social formation as a new cognitive paradigm that brings forth a new language capable of theorizing onto-political meanings of liminal beings. Chang demonstrates a possibility of such theorization by examining Wu Ming-Yi's The Man with the Compound Eyes: “The Man assembles different ways of knowing to imagine planetary connection from the islands of Taiwan and the Pacific.” In the story, not only an imaginary county in Taiwan but also Indigenous Austronesian peoples as well as nonhuman creatures play central roles in invoking the multiplicity of Taiwan's settler colonial formation and environmental injustices. In The Man, according to Chang, human existence poses a destructive threat to the existential memories of other creatures as well as of their own. It foregrounds the vision that “no life can survive without other lives, without the ecological memories other living creatures have, memories of the environments in which they live.” In this regard, Chang's reading of The Man has much resonance with Wang's analysis of The Stolen Bicycle as an attempt to articulate post-anthropocentric memories and their role in a radical rethinking of given onto-epistemological paradigms.The fourth group analyzes malleable power. Lorenzo Andolfatto's “Semantics of Tea Drinking: Online Writing and the Shaping of Counter-public Spheres in Xi Jinping's China” examines what Foucault calls “capillary” forms of state power in China's everyday governance under Xi Jinping. He approaches this issue by closely reading online texts that present people's bei hecha (being asked for tea) experiences. Bei hecha or hecha (drinking tea) are expressions commonly used to imply being approached by the State Security Police for a forced appointment and interrogation. Andolfatto unpacks not only the intricacies of the state's surveillance and mode of everyday governmentality but also people's counter-public spheres of dissent by analyzing hecha ji texts (written recollection of tea-drinking sessions) where they share their bei hecha experiences. Hecha practice reflects, according to Andolfatto, the state police's “hybrid” orientation within the Chinese legal field vis-à-vis the law and the government's directives, which is best represented by the policy of “stability preservation.” Hecha developed as a method of “preemptive authoritarian” intervention into people's everyday lives to ensure stability preservation and was adopted at the local level by a police force to implement the methodical “decomposition” of internal dissent. But at the same time, Andolfatto concludes, hecha ji writing offers a tool for the reconstitution of surveilled voices into a “counter-public sphere” or “oppositional community” (Felski 1989: 168) through its shared articulation of oppression, harassment, and fear.Hans Steinmüller's “Shanzhai: Creative Imitation of China in Highland Myanmar” looks at the Wa State in contemporary Myanmar to unpack the material and symbolic implications of creative imitation or appropriation of China's ideological and political policies. Central to Steinmüller's inquiry is shanzhai (mountain fortress), a term that is commonly used to describe creative and ironic brand imitation in the People's Republic of China today. The Wa State, being a “literal” mountain fortress located between China and Myanmar, has been called a cheap copy, a miniature version of China. It has adopted a pragmatic imitation of China for its own survival in the cases of Maoism, authoritarian capitalism, and ethnic identity-formation. Tracing the history of the Wa State's close relationship with China in the areas of economy and military, Steinmüller discusses the pragmatic limitations and possibilities of the Wa's strategic decisions in following China as its model and ally. He concludes that the Wa State's “imitation” “tends to follow practical contingencies, rather than paradigmatic similarities,” exemplified in its adoption of Maoism and capitalism. In this sense, the commonsensical distinction between the original and the copy embedded in the essentialist conception of imitation does not help us understand the Wa State's appropriation of China and the malleable nature of its power.

papers.title: Irrigation water conservation and market- based approaches: balancing agricultural and urban water demands in the face of climate change in Jordan’s Azraq RAED A L - TABINI , OCTAVIO A . RAMIREZ ,
papers.title_normalized: irrigation water conservation and market based approaches balancing agricultural and urban water demands in the face of climate change in jordan s azraq raed a l tabini octavio a ramirez
papers.abstract: Climate change is the one of the most challenging environmental problems facing people in Jordan, with far-reaching impacts on the economy, public health, water resources, infrastructure, coastal resources, energy demand, natural features and recreation (Davies, 1958). In Jordan, growing impacts of climate change also come at a time when water resources are already under stress due to existing scarcity that is magnified by demands from a growing population and rising per capita incomes. While Jordan has several projects under way, like the Red Sea-Dead Sea Canal, to meet this demand for water, other adaptation measures could be taken to reduce the use of the nation’s renewable and non-renewable water. This chapter explores the potential utility of market institutions as a form of adaptation that can promote a sustainable future for water resources in Jordan and thus to help adapt to a potential reduction of water availability due to climate change and/or increased climate variability. Institutions, however, are often insufficient by themselves. The best adaptations and solutions may require changes in behaviour toward sustainable management practices of river basins. Ultimately, it is water user behaviour that will define the water profile consumption of a given region. In this light, sustainable changes are best achieved through a combination of widespread institutional adjustment as well as targeted local programmes. This chapter examines Jordan’s Azraq Basin in the Mafraq Governorate, which also includes parts of the Zarqa, Hamad and Sirhan Basins (Figure 19.1). It identifies economically efficient measures that could conserve water in irrigated agriculture, while also sustaining the growing urban water demands of nearby Amman. This map shows water basins in Jordan with the Azraq Basin in the middle, just east of Amman. Innovative solutions may have far-reaching applications. If effective institutions and behaviour adjustments are successful, they may be implemented in other countries to help adapt to water shortages abroad. As the global population is expected to exceed 9 billion by 2050, innovations that influence the behaviour of water users will be necessary to balance global food security with increased stress on natural water endowments. It is also important to recognize that achieving sustainable water management will be difficult to balance with Jordan’s national goals of rural poverty reduction and national food security; Hope et al. (2008) identified similar policy conflicts between irrigation and urban water uses for South Africa, while Giordano (2007) and Han and Zhao (2007) observed this kind of conflict in China. Consequently, innovations in Jordan may provide useful examples for water user behaviour in other countries. When adaptation to climate variability disrupts livelihoods, science becomes part of the political debate. Even in the status quo, population and climate pressures are increasing the competition for fresh water (Aggarwal, 2000; Akpabio, 2007; Ward, 2007). Nowhere is this more striking than in the Middle East (Arar, 1991; AlWeshah, 2000; Salman et al., 2008). Jordan, a mostly landlocked country bordering Palestine, Israel, Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Syria, has been plagued by water scarcity since ancient times (Brooks, 1993; Scott et al., 2003; Mohsen, 2007). Due to its dry climate and scant rainfall, water scarcity is still a serious environmental challenge facing Jordan (Figure 19.2) and is a central factor defining, promoting and limiting Jordan’s population, resources and economy. For example, more than 90 per cent of Jordan’s land area receives less than 200 mm of rainfall per year (Chebaane et al., 2004; Al-Kharabsheh and Ta’any, 2005). While water resources in Jordan have either stagnated or varied incrementally each year, its population continues to rise. A high rate of natural population growth, combined with sporadic large inflows of refugees, has altered the balance between population and water. The old balance, which lasted to 1950, has gradually changed to a chronic and worsening imbalance. Jordan’s water situation is challenged by the constraint that Jordan shares much of its surface water resources with neighbouring countries, whose control limits Jordan’s supplies (Ramirez et al., 2010). Excessive pumping from the Jordan aquifer by Israel exerts pressure on Jordan’s groundwater resources, while accelerated well and dam building in Syria has reduced the amount of water flowing south on the Yarmouk River (Humpal et al., 2012). Jordan’s major water resources are groundwater, surface water and treated wastewater effluent. The total renewable safe yield of groundwater resources in all of Jordan is an estimated 275 million cubic metres (MCM) per year. Water use from these renewable sources has exceeded the safe renewable supplies by more than 200 MCM per year in recent years, a pattern that cannot be sustained without water imports, recycling, reuse, virtual water or reduced demand (Ramirez et al., 2010). Jordan’s water scarcity will present growing technical and policy challenges over the next two decades as the forecasted population doubles, living standards rise (Alkhaddar et al., 2005; Jordan Ministry of Water and Irrigation, 2009) and climate change risks result in increasingly uncertain and variable precipitation. Furthermore, because many of Jordan’s poor are migrating to urban areas, these people face growing food and water insecurity (Faruqui and Al-Jayyousi, 2002). Additionally, high domestic water demands are exacerbated by large numbers of foreigners in Jordan. According to a March 2008 report by the Integrated Regional Information Networks of the United Nations (IRIN, 2008) the arrival of 500,000 Iraqi refugees since 2003 has compounded Jordan’s water problem. Jordan also hosts nearly 300,000 Egyptian guest workers, 200,000 Syrians and other expatriates, including an estimated 167,000 Palestinian refugees. As a result of the civil war in neighbouring Syria, more than 550,000 Syrian refugees are also in Jordan (UNHCR, 2013). Increased urban water demand, poor management by current well-users, expensive profit-for-drop irrigation measures, increased salinity from industrial runoff and climate change all compound these problems. United States Agency for International Development (USAID) estimates show that, within the next few decades, Jordan’s annual water resources per capita are expected to fall to just 90 m3 (Humpal et al., 2012). As climate change is expected to raise the average temperature in Jordan uniformly by 3°C in the winter and 4.5°C in the summer, with no marked change in precipitation (Harrison, 2009), drought conditions will magnify this scarcity, reduce available urban water supply and disproportionately harm rural agricultural and grazing communities who need reliable rainfall to grow crops and raise livestock. Jordan has recently examined numerous measures for coping with these shortages: in December 2013, a MoU was signed with Israel and Palestine to implement the first phase of the Red Sea-Dead Sea Water Conveyance Project in order to tackle the chronic water shortage. The Red Sea-Dead Sea Canal Project will convey water by canal from the Red Sea to the Dead Sea and provide 850 MCM of potable water after desalination. The project is aimed to assist the Dead Sea, the water level of which has been falling since the 1960s (Akash and Mohsen, 1998; Salman et al., 2001), mostly as a result of upstream surface water diversions and industrial evaporation ponds. One important new source of water to help alleviate water shortages in Amman is the US$1 billion Disi Water Project (Figure 19.3). Originally contracted in October 2007, it includes construction of a 325 km pipeline that will pump water from the Disi aquifer to Amman (Enerji, 2009). However, without major changes, these proposed projects have been called merely ‘breathing space’ that will, in the end, fail to meet the ‘ever-growing water deficit that looms on the 18-20 year time horizon’ (Humpal et al., 2012). Jordan’s Azraq Aquifer accounts for a large part of its underground water resources (Bajjali and Al-Hadidi, 2006). As of 2010, most of the extraction was devoted to irrigation through pumping, as previously approved by Jordan’s government. While the government may have legal authority to rescind some or all of the pumping permits, farmers view the permits as long-term water rights. In light of these debates, policy makers have considerable interest in any information concerning what factors influence water use and water use efficiency by farmers who pump from this aquifer. Policy and decision makers also need information that can help meet the needs of individual farmers, as well as help inform better water policy choices. Because the Azraq Aquifer is close to Amman, a major policy objective in regard to the aquifer is to examine the economic feasibility of water transfers by reallocating pumping from irrigation to urban water use to support Amman’s growth. This increased pressure on agricultural water use in Jordan comes at a time when rural poverty reduction and national food security are major national goals. An important water policy aim of Jordan is to minimize the economic impact on farmers and on the overall economic welfare of this region’s people, resulting from the increased water conservation that will be required of irrigated agriculture (Doppler et al., 2002).

papers.title: Searching for Peace: A Memoir of Israel By EhudOlmert. Brookings Institution Press, 2022. 352 pages. $27.99, hardcover.
papers.title_normalized: searching for peace a memoir of israel by ehudolmert brookings institution press 2022 352 pages 27 99 hardcover
papers.abstract: On December 1, 2003, Ehud Olmert, then second in command to Prime Minister Ariel Sharon, gave a remarkable speech at a memorial ceremony for David Ben-Gurion. He quoted Ben-Gurion's 1949 statement to the Knesset, following ceasefire agreements that ended the previous year's Arab-Israeli war: “When the question arose of having all the land of Israel without a Jewish state, or a Jewish state without the entire land of Israel—we chose a Jewish state without the land.” Olmert continued, in his own words, “Two decades later, Ben-Gurion declared, after he was already a retired statesman, that in exchange for a real peace Israel would need to give away the great majority of the territory it had conquered in the Six Day War [of 1967]. Since then, much water has flowed. Facts were set on the ground…but the bloody conflict with the Palestinians has never ended. It's time to end it” (167–68). What made the speech remarkable was the fact that Olmert was a longtime hardliner on the Arab-Israeli conflict, in general, and the Palestinian issue, in particular. He had long opposed any Israeli withdrawal from its 1967 territorial conquests, as well as all Arab proposals for peace, the Oslo Accords of 1993 and 1995, and the 2000 Camp David negotiations. As mayor of Jerusalem, he subscribed to the Likud party view that there had to be a “united, undivided Jerusalem under eternal Israel sovereignty.” Acting on that belief, he aggressively expanded the Jewish settlements in East Jerusalem. However, in March 2006, Olmert was elected prime minister. In subsequent speeches, he not only reiterated his 2003 support for the return of most of the territories Israel conquered in 1967 in exchange for peace with the leading Arab states, but he also called for a two-state solution. This would be possible, he said, when the Palestinians ended terrorism and agreed to border modifications that would allow Israel to retain some of its West Bank settlements. If they accept these terms, Olmert said, “I will invite Abu Mazen [Mahmoud Abbas, head of the Palestinian Authority] to meet me immediately in order to conduct a real, open, genuine and serious dialogue between us…[resulting in] an independent and viable Palestinian state.”1 How do you stop ruling over another people? How do you stop depriving them of basic rights and going on as if nothing is wrong….There was no choice but to give up on land in Judea and Samaria (64-65). If we succeeded, great. If not, we would unilaterally withdraw from the great majority of the West Bank, including parts of municipal Jerusalem….But what I really wanted was a negotiated, comprehensive peace deal with the Palestinians (196, 269). What made this a possibility, Olmert argues, was the death of Yasser Arafat in November 2004 and his replacement by Abbas as the most important Palestinian leader. Arafat, Olmert claims, “had given up on achieving any negotiated settlement….He had taken advantage of the Oslo Accords to prepare for further bloodshed, and had rejected [Prime Minister] Ehud Barak's generous offers and chosen instead to launch the Second Intifada” (270). By contrast, Olmert continues, “Abbas turned against the terrorist organizations and spoke out against terror. And it wasn't just lip service in English, the way it had been with Arafat” (270). There is no doubt that Abbas was more forthright than Arafat in rejecting terrorism—or any form of violent resistance to the occupation—and wholeheartedly accepting a two-state settlement. Nonetheless, Olmert's argument is simplistic and is rejected by most serious historians.3 The most persuasive accounts hold that the Israeli defeat of Egypt and Syria in the 1973 war convinced Arafat that the Palestinians could not rely either on their military forces or those of the wider Arab world. Consequently, he realized that the best hope would be a compromise, two-state settlement. Over the next few years, then, the strategy of the Palestinian Liberation Organization (PLO) gradually changed to give priority to negotiations over guerrilla warfare and terrorism. This culminated in the PLO's November 1988 announcement that it recognized Israel and accepted its right to exist. The organization would therefore seek only the creation of a Palestinian state in the West Bank and Gaza, with Arab East Jerusalem as its capital. Further, the PLO agreed that the new state would be largely demilitarized, would welcome the stationing of international peacekeeping forces along its borders to ensure demilitarization and peace, and would end terrorism and all forms of attack on Israel from its territory. As Olmert suggests, until his discussions with Abbas, the 1993–95 Oslo Accords between Israel (led by Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and Foreign Minister Shimon Peres) and Arafat, followed by the 2000 Camp David talks between Barak and Arafat, were the most promising efforts to reach a two-state settlement. Their failure, however, was at least as much the fault of the Israelis as it was of Arafat.4 That first meeting had dramatic implications for two main reasons. First, it created a positive atmosphere between the two teams. It would take some time for that to turn into friendship and trust, but the first meeting laid the groundwork for genuine discussions rather than arguments, finger pointing, and unflattering leaks. Second, both sides were given the opportunity to lay out their expectations. I had no interest in another round of posturing. I wanted to negotiate for real (269). In the ensuing discussions with Abbas, Olmert set out his positions on the central issues of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. These are summarized in his memoirs. “I made clear to Abbas that I accepted the principle of returning to the 1967 borders,” Olmert writes. “Implementing it, however, would require some adjustments….I said we would annex about 6 per cent of the territory and give them the same amount of land within Israel” (280, 290). However, “the territory” meant only the West Bank, not Gaza. When we looked at the maps, it was clear we would be hard pressed to come up with that much territory to give in exchange. Of course, we could offer areas in the desert south of the Gaza Strip or in the Judaean desert. But the Palestinians weren't interested in inarable land. What you give us, they said, needs to be of equal value to what you're taking (290). As expected, Olmert insisted that a Palestinian state would have to be demilitarized, allowed only a minimally armed police force capable of maintaining internal order. Further, the state could not enter into alliances or military treaties with any country that had no relations with Israel, which would continue to have military outposts on the mountaintops in the West Bank. An international peacekeeping force would be stationed along the Palestinian state's eastern border with Jordan, and Israel would control the airspace over the state, which would be denied an airport of its own. Moreover, the Israeli army would be allowed to cross into the West Bank state should a foreign army (i.e., Syria, Iraq, or Iran) approach the river boundary between Israel and Jordan. Finally, he says, “Israel would have the right to defend itself against terrorism…[which] would not be constrained by any territorial limitations” (287). This meant forces could enter the West Bank whenever Israel deemed it necessary to fight what it defined as “terrorism.” According to Olmert, Abbas accepted that the new state would have to be “demilitarized,” though he is careful not to claim that the Palestinian leader accepted all of the demands. It is true that for a number of years, Abbas and other Palestinian leaders accepted the principle of demilitarization—preferring to call it “non-militarization”—but how much Abbas would agree to Olmert's entire “security” package would undoubtedly have been in question had the Olmert-Abbas negotiations continued. In his memoirs, Olmert claims he “understood” and sympathized with the suffering of the Palestinian refugees from the 1948 war. He even accepts that “there were more than a few cases” of Palestinian families who “were driven from their homes and lands and lost their property.” Moreover, he writes, “it is even reasonable to speak of reparations,” although not from Israel but instead “from nations of the world who want to be part of bringing a solution of justice and peace” (286–87). Olmert deserves credit for being the first if not the only leading Israeli official to admit at least partial Israeli responsibility for what today is widely called “the Nakba,” though he does not use that term and insists that “recognition of suffering is not the same as accepting blame.” It is unlikely that the refugee problem would have blocked an Israeli-Palestinian peace settlement if agreement on the other issues had been reached, for Abbas—and even Arafat—had long recognized that the official demand that all refugees be allowed to return to Israel had no chance of acceptance. They were prepared to accept a symbolic return of far fewer than the estimated 750,000 to 1 million refugees from the 1948 and 1967 wars, together with some acknowledgment of Israeli responsibility for their plight. “I need something symbolic on the subject of refugees,” Olmert says Abbas told him. “I don't want to change the nature of the State of Israel” (273). In their talks, Abbas asked Israel to accept 100,000 refugees over five years. Olmert countered with an offer to accept 5,000, as long as it was not based on any “right of return”—long a Palestinian demand—and was subject to an Israeli veto over how many and who would be allowed. The numbers were negotiable. Olmert writes, “I was prepared to take as many as 15,000 refugees, if Abbas had demanded it” (291). Other accounts report that Olmert would have accepted 30,000 over 10 years. The relatively small difference in numbers suggests that the issue was bridgeable, as a number of Israeli and Palestinian officials have concluded.5 In past negotiations, one of the major issues was how the fresh-water aquifers in the West Bank would be divided. Abbas told Olmert it was crucial that Israel evacuate the settler-dominated city of Ariel, located some 12 miles inside the West Bank, especially because it sat on a major water aquifer. As well, other Israeli settlements in the West Bank had been built in part because of their access to and control over water sources. While refusing to evacuate Ariel, Olmert told Abbas that, quite soon, water would no longer be scarce in the region because five new desalination plants were to be built, producing enough drinkable water to meet not only Israel's needs but also those of the Palestinians. “We have no problem building one or two plants that will provide all the water the Palestinians will need,” he said, “[and which] will be under absolute control of the Palestinians” (289). Abbas “never again raised the issue of water,” Olmert asserts, and while other Palestinian and Israeli negotiators continued the discussion, “it became a trivial point in the talks.” The desalination plants were built, the former prime minister continues, which along with other new technologies did “completely solve Israel's endemic water shortages” (333). As mayor of Jerusalem, Olmert held vigorously to the standard Israeli position that the city was the eternal capital of Israel and would never again be divided. However, he writes, he came to believe that this was untenable, so he proposed to Abbas that the city be partitioned or “shared,” as he preferred to put it. The Israeli areas—predominantly in West Jerusalem but also in a number of Jewish neighborhoods that had been established in the East after 1967—would remain under Israeli sovereignty. The Palestinians would be given authority over what remained of Arab East Jerusalem, which could also become the capital of the proposed state. Neither Israel nor the Palestinians would have control over the Old City, the Temple Mount, and other parts of religious significance to Islam, Judaism, and Christianity. Those areas would be internationalized and governed by a UN-sponsored commission that would guarantee freedom of movement and worship for all. There is no question that this was a remarkable proposal, going far beyond any other Israeli leader, before or since. There was, however, one unresolved issue that could have killed the entire deal: By 2008, there were almost 200,000 Jewish settlers in East Jerusalem.6 “The Jewish neighborhoods built after 1967 would remain in Israeli sovereignty, and would be included in the 6.3 percent of annexed territory,” Olmert writes (294). He is silent on precisely how East Jerusalem could be turned over to Palestinian “sovereignty” while the Jewish settlers—already approaching half the area's population—would not only remain in place but continue to be part of Israel. Olmert's negotiations with Abbas did not include the future of Gaza, controlled by Hamas. In contrast to his position on reaching a two-state agreement with the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank, Olmert categorically refused to negotiate with the group, explaining that it is “a terror organization that absolutely refuses to accept the existence of Israel….I do not believe there is any possibility of a political arrangement with Hamas,” he says. “There was no chance I'd talk with them” (331, 260). This categorical refusal to negotiate, together with several Israeli strikes on Hamas targets in Gaza, resulted in an escalating series of tit-for-tat military attacks. Then, in December 2008, Olmert ordered a major assault on Hamas and Gaza. Operation Cast Lead included a ground invasion as well as massive air and artillery strikes, not merely on Hamas positions but on the economic and civil infrastructure of Gaza. Some 1,400 Palestinians, two-thirds of them noncombatants, were killed—not to mention the long-term, human costs of the infrastructure attacks.7 The international criticism of Israeli aerial assaults in Gaza is largely unfounded. What would any other country do if hundreds of thousands of its citizens were targeted by thousands of rockets over so many years?….Israel has no choice but to defend itself against a terror organization that actively targets our civilians (331). This “self-defense” argument is unpersuasive. The Israeli attacks, designed to maintain the indirect occupation and economic siege of Gaza, cannot be considered “self-defense,” especially in light of Hamas overtures that Israel—in particular, Olmert—had rejected. To be sure, there were ambiguities and inconsistencies in the Hamas positions, but the way to resolve them was to enter into negotiations. No serious peace proposal called on Israel to withdraw from its occupied territories, direct or indirect, unless and until a reasonable and enforceable political settlement was reached. In short, a state cannot persuasively claim a right to self-defense if attacks on it are a consequence of occupation and repression. While no formal agreements have been reached between Hamas and Israel, for a number of years there has been a truce—most likely, not merely a tacit one. In return for the group's ending its attacks on Israel and making serious efforts to prevent more militant groups, like Islamic Jihad, from using Gaza as a base for assaults, Israel not only has ended any efforts to overthrow the regime in Gaza but has accepted—and by all signs approved—economic assistance to Hamas, including straight cash transfers from Gulf Arab states. The explanation for this unacknowledged but unmistakable truce is quite clear: Hamas has given up its earlier goal of defeating Israel and establishing its rule over all of Palestine. Israeli military and security leaders, uninterested in conquering Gaza, now view a Hamas-ruled Gaza, committed to preventing Islamic Jihad attacks on Israel, as a force for stability.10 At least as important, the often-violent rivalry between the Palestinian Authority and PLO in the West Bank and Hamas in Gaza is another major obstacle to the reunification of the two areas and a negotiated two-state settlement that most Israeli leaders continue to oppose. Consider the irony of Israeli policies today. To kill any chances for a two-state settlement, Israel is more willing to make political deals (tacit or explicit) with Hamas than with the Palestinian Authority. In effect, then, it favors a group that—notwithstanding the recent moderation—has a history of violence and religious fundamentalism over compromise with the more secular and moderate Abbas, whose long-held and repeatedly demonstrated commitment to nonviolence and compromise is not open to question. On September 16, 2008, Olmert met with Abbas and presented his plan on territory and borders, land swaps, security, Jerusalem, and refugees.
