papers.title: Oppressive Destinations: From The Lost Traveler's Tour Guide
papers.title_normalized: oppressive destinations from the lost traveler s tour guide
papers.abstract: Oppressive DestinationsFrom The Lost Traveler's Tour Guide Alexander Weinstein (bio) The Island of Trilage A love exists on the island of Trilage for all that spins. Here you'll find pinwheels aflutter in front yards, clacking spokes of bicycles studded with playing cards, roulette wheels whirling in casinos, and toy shops selling yoyos and spinning tops. Every clock in Trilage has a frenetic second hand, relentlessly circling past the hours as if attempting to win a race it can never conquer, and by doing so, it perfectly imitates the lives of its citizens. For, on the island of Trilage, everyone is busy. Mornings are filled with the clatter of men and women rushing through kitchens, coffeemakers percolating, tea kettles screaming, as they hurry to feed the dog, iron their slacks, inhale breakfasts, and tear off in their cars for work. Around the island, shop owners prepare windows for the holidays or clear them for the next sales event. Angry motorists idle at red lights, policemen place tickets beneath the wipers of parked cars, workers rush to lunches, overworked parents do last minute grocery shopping, lovers hurry to dinner dates, and friends down a single-malt before running home. Playdates are arranged for children months in advance, only to be cancelled last minute, birthday cards are sent a week late, and every social occasion is buckshot with apologies. So sorry we never got back to you. I've been meaning to call! He's been so busy. You know how it is. On Trilage, everyone wishes they could rest for a moment, long enough to have a glass of wine, plant a garden, take a vacation—but they never have the time: there's still laundry to fold, weddings to plan for, houses to paint, and lawns to mow. Next summer they'll finally take that vacation, they promise, and they roll up their sleeves and dive into a project which will consume the next decade of their lives. This is why, despite all the hours, funds, and sleepless nights which The Trilage Bureau of Travel has spent trying to increase tourism to the area, their efforts prove unsuccessful. Those who visit the island, feel like lost goslings as they jump out of the way of impatient drivers, cringe from surly waiters, and cram into buses amid pushy men and rude women. They've left the island vowing never to return. Indeed, why anyone would ever book a trip to Trialge is a complete mystery to us; it's exactly like our hometowns. [End Page 77] The Country of Abnök In the dusty halls of the National Library one can still find the country's original maps. They've been there among the dark desks of the Law Library where old men turn onion-skinned pages, raise a finger to their lips, and tell you to shush. A large globe sits in the corner of the map room, ringed by a heavy brass stand which shuns its purpose with a printed sign: Do Not Touch. And there, behind the glass cases are the yellowed edges of the maps. Look closely, and you'll discover that, before Abnök, there was just an expanse of hills and plains and a river which now runs through the country's center. Who constructed Abnök's borders? Schoolbooks tell the story of Archmanz, a man who prior to Abnök's creation was known for his small hands and an ability to build walls. He began by recruiting workers to build a wall around his hut, then a wall around his neighbor's, and soon he recruited more workers to build walls around the wheat fields and walls around the cattle. There were complaints from friends and family, but Archmanz rewarded his workers with stores of grain and jugs of cream, and soon Archmanz's walls expanded like ripples from a cast stone. It was then that Archmanz announced his plan for The Great Wall. Soon, many came to help mix the mortar and stack the bricks until the wall stretched from the forests of the South to the mountains of the North. Archmanz crowned himself king then, and he turned...

papers.title: The Study on the Cultural Changes in the Qiang Diet in the Resettlement Area in Qionglai
papers.title_normalized: the study on the cultural changes in the qiang diet in the resettlement area in qionglai
papers.abstract: The old Qiang stockaded villages, Zhitai Village and Kuapo Village,were located in mountainous area with an altitude of more than 2,000 meters. Both the economic and transportation conditions were poor there. The source of income for the people in Zhitai Village and Xige of Kuapo Village came mainly from planting and collecting wild herbs. The main agriculture product was corn,but they also planted potatoes and cabbage. Chickens,cows and goats were raised by every family. 1. The change in living location After the Wenchuan earthquake in 2008,the Qiang victims in these two villages were all moved, on 23 Setptember 2009,to Youzha Township and Nanbaoshan Township in Qionglai where we find today’ s Zhitai Village ( Area D) and Muti Village ( Area C) in the resettlement areas . Youzha Township and Nanbaoshan Township are located northwest of Qionglai ,bordering with Dachuan Town in Baoshan County,Ya’ an Municipality. Nanbaoshan Township is a big forestry village in Qionglai. It is very rich in natural resources. Forest coverage reaches 94% ,and is characterized by biological diversity. Youzha Township is also rich in natural resources,and has fertile land. The facilities at the Nanbaoshan resettlement area are perfect,and moreover,experts provide guidance to the people on how to plant tea trees,and manage the tea plantations. 2. Change of diet culture andan explanation of the geographical conditions The Qiang area in Northwest Sichuan is mountainous and crossed by many rivers. The rainfall is moderate. The area is suitable for the growth of crops. The main crops are corn,wheat,barley and potato,but they also grow beans and vegetables.There is a amount of rice production in the southeastern part of the area. The most symbolic foods in the traditional Qiang diet are Zhengzhengfan,( a kind of steamed rice) Yangyuciba ( potatoe sticky rice cake) ,zhubiaorou ( fatty pork) and za wine. Before the earthquake,the staple food of the Qiangs was corn,and rice was purchased. The potato was both a staple and vegetable. Vegetables also included lots of wild herbs. Meats were mainly fatty pork and chicken and sheep which they raised. Some meat had to be bought. As for drinks,za wine and barley wine were drunk in daily life. After the earthquake,the main starch staple became rice,whereas before it was corn. Non seasonal vegetables became popular. The fatty pork ( zhubiaorou) that they made in the past was difficult to find,so now they mainly ete pork, mutton,chicken,carp and seafood. They mainly drank beer and spirits,and not the traditional za wine and barley beer. With the changes of living environment in the resettlement,production conditions of the Qiang changed. For example,not only was the humidity too high in the resettlement area for making the traditional salted fatty pork,the government placed a ban on raising livestock in the village because they wanted to develop local tourism. This situation reduced the amount and variety of meat eaten by the people. Thus,for the Qiang who had lived in the old villages for generations,change in their living location resulted in a change in their traditional diet which had evolved as part of their geography and environment. 3. The Culture of Diet culture within the geo regional and industrial interactive space Before the earthquake, the Qiang villages were remote and sealed off from the outside. MostQiang lived a self sufficient life. The circulation of people and material was small. After the resettlement,in order to integrate into local social networks and guarantee the development of the Qiang village itself,they needed to communicate more with the outside. After resettlement,transportation developed a lot. At the same time,tourism development stimulated the local people to go outside, and people from the outside to go in. This kind of communication can gradually influence the eating habits of local people. The Qiang changed from being self – sufficient to having a surplus for selling. With the improvement of productivity,the adjustment of economic structure,and the improvement of transportation conditions,the villagers relied more on the central markets,and contact with the surrounding ethnic groups became closer. Moreover,the feedback effect between different cultures became more prominent,as with the culture of diet where it has been shown that the centerflows to the frontier,for example, when people living in towns or cities come to a Qiang villages choose to eat Qiang snacks such as Yangyuciba ( potato sticky rice cakes) . Therefore,if we analyze a local society ’ s great traditionand small traditionfrom the perspective of markets,we see an increased dependence on thecenter. If we analyze the mutual penetration of different culture circles from the perspective of culture,we see that it forms a mutual feedback type of pattern. This feedback will not only change the daily diet,but also the way of life and social structure of Qiang society. 4. The Restoration  of a culturally traditional diet and ethnic identity After resettlement,when tourism was promoted by the local government,the Qiang realized the importance of their ethnic uniqueness , which prompted a kind of restorationof their traditional culture . Thisrestorationembodied the Qiang people’ s sublation of diet culture. The eating culture of the Qiang and their social culture is,in a way,related to their past, present and future. The reconstruction of theQiang’ s traditional diet culture in the resettlement area indicates more a sense of ethnic identity. Therefore,when the Han people and other ethnic people ( tourists) enter the restructured living spaces,an explicit symbol that can be used to distinguish oneself from others is manifested in the culture of eating. No matter if we explain this cultural phenomenon from other’ s or our own perspective, it has already implied that whether a Qiang individual eat Yangyuciba, Zhubiaorou or drink zajiu wine is not only a matter of eating habits,but it is also an explicit marker and symbol which distinguishes themselves from other ethnic groups. 5. Industrialized food coming from the outside and and changes of social lifestyle With an increased understanding of outside information, knowing more about industrialized products via TV etc. ,and having more contact with Han people,the eating habits of the Qiang people in the resettlement areas are gradually changing. This kind of change is especially obvious with teenagers. For example,instead of drinking zajiu wine,more people choose to drink beer. Zajiu wine is a specific wine of the Qiang and also an identity marker of the Qiang,and moreover,by drinking beer,ethnic differences are weakened. Therefore,in the social networks,beer,as an industrialized product,is not only a kind of beverage,but also a lifestyle ,a medium being used on social occasions, and a symbol that has lots of symbolic meaning. With the constant fusion and development of modern society,new things are formed more and more rapidly,and people’ s ability to accept new objects also improves quickly. After the May 12 th Wenchuan earthquake,the Qiang ’ s traditional food culture was impacted dramatically. Under these impacts,not only should the Qiang try to maintain their traditional culture,but also should strive to survive within modern society.

papers.title: Folklore in Utah: A History and Guide to Resources (review)
papers.title_normalized: folklore in utah a history and guide to resources review
papers.abstract: Reviewed by: Folklore in Utah: A History and Guide to Resources James Leary Folklore in Utah: A History and Guide to Resources. Edited by David Stanley . 2004. Logan: Utah State University Press. 360 pages. ISBN: 0874215889 (soft cover). Book covers, if well-considered, combine words and images succinctly to convey content in both straightforward and allusive fashions. "Folklore [End Page 193] in," and therefore not exclusively of, Utah connotes pluralism, while "A History and Guide to Resources" heralds an interpretive chronology and contemporary handbook. As for images, on the front cover, sandwiched between title and subtitle, Austin Fife adjusts a disc-cutting recorder in 1949 for Mrs. B. Walker, a guitar-wielding singer. The back cover includes an expected summary blurb, alongside a photograph of Mary Holiday Black, a Navajo, at work on a basket. Both images are bordered in white, suggesting photographic paper, snapshot origins, and archival deposition. The images likewise show and signal an inclusive consideration of gender, genre, cultures, field research, and public presentation. In his engagingly thoughtful preface, editor David Stanley elaborates: "Folklore work in Utah has been characterized from the very beginning by a similar breaking down of boundaries," between Mormons and non-Mormon "Gentiles," European and Native Americans, native-born Utahns and recent immigrants, "folk" and folklorists, and academic and public folklorists. Twenty-six essays in four sections follow. Parts I and II offer an intellectual history of Utah folklorists and folklorists in Utah, beginning with "The First Folklorists," including Austin and Alta Fife, Wayland Hand, and Helen Papanikolas, who pioneered in the study of Greek and other ethnic groups. Subsequently, "The Second and Third Generation of Folklorists" appropriately devotes an essay each to such influential second-generation figures as William A. "Bert" Wilson, Barre Toelken, and Jan Brunvand, followed by a single essay sketching the lives and work of two dozen third-generation folklorists whose ongoing efforts concern the folklore of Mormons, American Indians, cowboys, diverse ethnic groups, and women, as well as the relationship between folklore and education, the environment, and archives. Section III, "Studies in Utah Folklore and Folklife," offers expected critical bibliographic essays on the study of Native American, Mormon, Latino, and ethnic folklore. Perhaps because of a slight tilt toward verbal, musical, and customary folklore, perhaps to emphasize the importance of comparative perspectives, these group-based overviews are augmented by essays on material culture and vernacular architecture. Section IV, devoted to public programs, commences with an astute portrayal of the emergence of public folklore in Utah by Elaine Thatcher that is particularly attentive to folk arts organizations. Six additional tightly-focused exegeses concern the role of the state humanities council, the Utah Folklore Society, and the Fife Folklore Conference, as well as the relationship of folklore to cultural tourism, federal and state parks, and assorted ethnic organizations. Four appendices ably guide readers to Utah's academic folklore programs, folklore archives, relevant museum collections, and community festivals. A bibliography of Utah folklore, listing nearly 1000 entries and accompanied by a comprehensive index, completes the volume. [End Page 194] Despite the participation of more than thirty contributors, each with their own voice, the essays are uniformly accessible, illuminating, and deeply humanistic, as evidenced by the deft prose portraits and more than sixty photographs of the remarkable people who have sustained and studied folklore in Utah. Beyond its obvious in-state audience, Folklore in Utah should appeal to folklorists compelled by the discipline's history and by the complex ways in which folklore in any given place engages universal issues. And grizzled folklorists recalling Metafolkloristica by the pseudonymous Franz Kinder and Boaz the Clown (who I suspect had a hand in this volume) will relish the jocular disciplinary reflexivity of awkward hulu dancing by David Stanley, Barre Toelken, Hal Cannon, and Steve Siporin, or of the legendary nocturnal scaling of Logan's River Heights bluff by David Hufford and Roger Welsch long before the advent of Polygamous Porter. All things considered, it is difficult to imagine a more ambitious, admirable, and authoritative volume devoted to folklore in an American state. James Leary University of Wisconsin Copyright © 2006 Department of Folklore and Ethnomusicology, Indiana University

papers.title: In memoriam: James Gordon Nelson 1932–2024
papers.title_normalized: in memoriam james gordon nelson 1932 2024
papers.authors: E. LeDrew; James S. Gardner; Bruce Mitchell
papers.abstract: Gordon Nelson, 2017, Cyprus Hills. Photo courtesy of Kathryn Nelson The first sentence Gordon Nelson published in a refereed journal is: “The Balsa is perhaps the most mysterious and controversial of primitive watercraft” (Nelson, 1961b, p. 157). This immediately evokes Gordon's desire to inquire about the unknown and to explore the complexities of the many dimensions of geography. Entitled “The geography of the Balsa,” this substantial article was published in the quarterly journal of maritime history, American Neptune (Nelson, 1961b). The journal's Editor provided the postscript “His specific interest in primitive watercraft centers on the extent to which they can serve as both means and evidence for early human migration and cultural development” (Nelson, 1961b, p. 195). This paper was followed by “Pre-European trade between Australia, Indonesia and the Asiatic Mainland” in The Canadian Geographer in 1961 (Nelson, 1961a). With these publications, Gordon had established a well-defined footprint in cultural geography. In 1965, however, he published a paper entitled “Some effects of glaciation on the Susquehanna River Valley” in the Annals of the Association of American Geographers (Nelson, 1965). Clearly, this was the start of an eclectic academic life and it did not happen by accident! Three significant influences can be identified. First, Gordon grew up less than two blocks from what Hamiltonians (Hamilton, Ontario) call “the Mountain,” which is actually a segment of the Niagara Escarpment. His curiosity about and love of nature started with many hours investigating the secrets of this environment by himself and with friends. His choice of graduate school at the University of Colorado was influenced by these early experiences and the possibility of seeing the “real” mountains (Shirley Nelson, pers. comm., 2024). Second, Gordon was accompanied in this journey by his wife and life-long companion, Shirley. Shirley provided support and contributed substance and style to much of Gordon's written work and professional activity. She is acknowledged in the first refereed journal article, “The geography of the Balsa” noted above. The book, Amid shifting sands (Nelson & Rghei, 2022) is dedicated to Shirley. During it all, including a number of moves of houses and home, they raised a family of three children who have gone on to professional careers and families of their own. Third, the concept of Landscape, inclusive of nature and humankind and their respective processes intertwined, was central to Gordon's interpretation of geographies, his practice of Geography as a scholarly discipline, and his public interest and activist work. He completed his undergraduate degree in Geography at McMaster University in 1955 and his Master's degree a year later at the University of Colorado. On his arrival for doctoral studies at Johns Hopkins University in 1956, he came into contact with two eminent scholar/scientists—George F. Carter and M. Gordon Wolman. The former was an archeologist/cultural geographer; the latter was a fluvial geomorphologist prominent for his leadership in process studies, including those associated with humankind. Gordon completed his PhD on the balsa and drift voyages with George Carter. Gordon Wolman also provided guidance to Gordon and perked a serious interest in geomorphology, leading to a post-doctoral fellowship at Johns Hopkins University that allowed Gordon to conduct research in the Susquehanna and Chemung Valleys. Thus, Gordon set forth into the academic world as what was called in those days “a well-rounded geographer,” with Landscape as an essential conceptual tool. Gordon joined the University of Alberta, Calgary, in the summer of 1960 as Assistant Professor of Geography at its new campus. A physical setting spanning the plains to the Canadian Rocky Mountains which contained a variety of land uses including national and provincial parks presented fertile ground for a field-oriented geographer. He led physical geographic projects in the Banff National Park headwaters of the Red Deer and Bow Rivers, exemplified in “Recession of the Hector and Peyto Glaciers: Further studies in the Drummond Glacier” (Brunger et al., 1967). Meanwhile, he was exploring the socio-historical aspects of fire in the Bow Valley of Banff National Park as seen in “Man as an instrument of landscape change: Fires, floods and national parks in the Bow Valley, Alberta” (Nelson & Byrne, 1966). His vision of landscape and landscape change was expansive and led to his book, The last refuge (Nelson, 1973) in which he chronicled the landscape and land use history of the Cypress Hills of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Within the university, he took an energetic interest in the ongoing institutional development and administration. Gordon served as Head of the Department of Geography from 1964 to 1967, Associate Dean in the Faculty of Arts from 1967 to 1970, and Assistant to the Vice-President (Academic) in 1970–1971. Under Gordon's leadership, the Department of Geography rapidly developed and in 1968, now with 13 academic staff, hosted the Annual Meeting of the Canadian Association of Geographers. Many of the principles that encouraged group interaction and public participation that became a hallmark of Gordon's career were honed during this period. He engaged the population on issues such as the proposed Winter Olympics, development of additional roads along valley bottoms, a new ski village at Lake Louise in Banff National Park, and development of National Park Initiatives including the Calgary-Banff Chapter (now Southern Alberta) of the National and Provincial Parks Association of Canada (now Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society). He had an “irrepressible enthusiasm” and “… his ability to knit facts and ideas in verbal presentation was magnetic” (Robert Scace, pers. comm., 2024). He shared authorship with his students and colleagues and this leaves a legacy of influential individuals who carry on with his ideas. From 1971 to 1975, Gordon was Professor of Geography at the University of Western Ontario (now Western University) and many issues associated with the environment of the Canadian shore of Lake Erie allowed him to further develop processes for the engagement of the public in resources management and decision making. These were structured on Gordon's “human ecological model” in which resource management problems were studied as an integration of ecology, technology, perceptions and attitudes, and institutional arrangements. One of his graduate students, James Battin, noted “He was a dynamic teacher/professor in the area of land use history and land use change. More importantly to our small group of graduate students he was approachable, intelligent and had a great sense of humour” (pers. comm., 2024). Reid Kreutzwiser, another student, noted “Gordon's commitment to mentoring students was undeniable, and his time in the field with his students was a highlight. We couldn't help but be inspired by his insights into the environment around us and human interaction with that environment. But perhaps most significant and inspiring … was his commitment to policy-relevant research” (pers. comm., 2024). A colleague at Western, Richard Butler, notes that “[Gordon's] appointment stimulated the development of courses in [resources management], attracted post-graduate students and led to the creation of an additional under-graduate degree programme, entitled Geography (Resources Management). He also enabled and supported the involvement of colleagues in a number of research projects, in my own case through his work with the Inuit Tapirisat with respect to tourism and national park development in the Arctic regions” (pers. comm., 2024). In 1975, Gordon was appointed Dean of the Faculty of Environmental Studies (now Faculty of Environment) and Professor of Geography at the University of Waterloo. He served as Dean until 1983. With his leadership, significant additions and modifications were made to the physical plant and the staffing arrangements of the constituent Departments. Most notably, the building was expanded to physically accommodate the School of Architecture in the Faculty. In addition, facilities were created for the rapidly emerging areas of geographical information systems and remote sensing, each of which had cross-disciplinary relevance and utility. As was the case at the University of Calgary, Gordon also continued to add to his research and public interest activities at the same time, typically through productive collaboration with colleagues and students. With colleagues John Theberge and Jamie Bastedo, he developed the ABC framework for management of human-environment issues. It involves understanding the abiotic, biotic, and cultural systems in an issue and that their integration is necessary to understand the many dimensions and interactions of a region which can then provide a “sense of place.” Many years of academic and community-based work within the ABC framework is gathered together in a compendium of papers entitled Places: Linking nature, culture, and planning (Nelson & Lawrence, 2009). This work “… ultimately translated into local, regional and provincial land use management approaches by government agencies, local authorities and communities, shaping the conversation, decision-making and policy to address this major issue impacting thousands of shoreline landowners and land use management agencies” (Patrick Lawrence, pers. comm. 2024). In 1983, he was appointed Professor in the Department of Urban and Regional Planning along with his appointment in Geography. In 1987, he founded the University of Waterloo Heritage Resources Centre. The engagement of students together with professional parks managers was the hallmark of the Heritage Resources Centre. The centre “… organized and ran many conferences involving professional parks and protected area managers at local, provincial/territorial and national levels all with the objective of bringing interested parties together and cultivating university-government partnerships” (John Theberge, pers. comm., 2024). In 1988, the Heritage Resources Centre was approached by a steering committee consisting of representatives of the Canadian Parks Service, the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources, and the Grand River Conservation Authority. The committee was developed to designate the Grand River as a Heritage River. With a group of post-graduate students, the Centre developed a “… compelling case for nominating the Grand River and its major tributaries and undertook a series of public engagement sessions to promote the designation among watershed communities … Gordon's commitment and active involvement in promoting the designation was instrumental in achieving this prestigious nomination for the river system” (Barbara Veale, pers. comm., 2024). Gordon's continuing engagement with the Grand River system resulted in a heritage landscape guide entitled The Grand River Watershed (Nelson et al., 2003). In 2004, he edited a book called Towards a grand sense of place: Writings on changing environments, land-uses, landscapes, lifestyles and planning of a Canadian Heritage River (Nelson et al., 2004) as a celebration of the 10th anniversary of the Grand as a Canadian Heritage River and the 20th anniversary of the Canadian Heritage Rivers System. Gordon retired from his professorial positions in Geography and Urban and Regional Planning at the University of Waterloo in 1997 and, in 1998, he was awarded the designation Distinguished Emeritus Professor. He continued in his role as Chair, Heritage Resources Centre until 2003. Two major projects occupied Gordon in his later retirement years. One of the great achievements of the parks and protected areas movement in Canada came to fruition in 2009 when the effort to expand the Nahanni National Park Reserve, first proposed in the early 1970s, was approved by the Government of Canada. Gordon was involved in the process through decades. In 2017, his book The magnificent Nahanni: The struggle to protect a wild place (Nelson, 2017) was published. In the Foreword, Harvey Locke writes that the book: “… contains reflections on this remarkable national park landscape by one of the keenest students of parks and protected areas this country has ever produced. For fifty years Gordon Nelson has been thinking about and influencing how the rest of us see national parks in Canada” (Nelson, 2017, p. xii). Gordon's long experience in institutional development and administration led to a consultancy at the Canadian University of Dubai in 2006. He reconnected with a former PhD student, Amer Rghei, at the American University in Dubai. Thrust into one of the most rapidly changing landscapes on earth, Gordon and Amer explored land use history and landscape change in the extreme. A result is the collaboration, Amid shifting sands (Nelson & Rghei, 2022). Therein, the landscape is viewed through time via its abiotic, biotic, and cultural components. Over 61 years, Gordon wove together many of the transdisciplinary threads of Geography with a focus on knowledgeable and effective management and conservation of the world around us. Gordon's interest was to “understand past and present relationships and interactions between human beings and their environments; his life's work had a focus on cause and effect in highly prized and inevitably vulnerable landscapes and habitats” (Robert Scace, pers. comm., 2024). He reached far beyond the borders of the academic environment to engage and foster public participation in these issues. In later years, his engagement of a wide network of friends and colleagues in a variety of working groups on a range of public environmental issues led a participant in one such group to refer to him as the “wise old owl” (Bill Caulfeild-Browne, pers. comm., 2024). His legacy has been carried forward by an army of former students, colleagues, collaborators, and friends who have benefitted from Gordon's intelligence, energy, and way of thinking and being in the world. Bill Caulfield-Browne wrote that “It was not just a pleasure working with Gordon but an education that I value to the day.” We are indebted to Shirley Nelson for providing and verifying details as well as identifying former students and colleagues. We thank Kathryn Nelson for providing the photograph. Many former students and colleagues have generously provided vignettes and comments regarding Gordon Nelson's impact on their careers which have added to the authors’ own personal experiences. We are grateful to: James Battin, James Battin Law Office, Tillsonburg, Ontario; Richard Butler, Emeritus Professor, Western University, Strathclyde Business School, Glasgow; Bill Caulfeild-Browne, Former Chair, The Nature Conservancy of Canada; Reid Kreutzwiser, Professor Emeritus, Department of Geography, Environment and Geomatics, University of Guelph; Patrick Lawrence, Chair & Professor, University of Toledo; Brian Luckman, Professor Emeritus, Western University; Robert Scace, President of Scace Environmental Advisors Inc., Calgary; John B. Theberge, Adjunct Professor, University of Waterloo; Barbara Veale, Acting Chief Administrative Officer, Conservation Halton; Gary Warrick, Professor Emeritus, Wilfrid Laurier University.

papers.title: The Old Chisholm Trail: From Cow Path to Tourist Stop by Wayne Ludwig
papers.title_normalized: the old chisholm trail from cow path to tourist stop by wayne ludwig
papers.abstract: Reviewed by: The Old Chisholm Trail: From Cow Path to Tourist Stop by Wayne Ludwig Sylvia Gann Mahoney The Old Chisholm Trail: From Cow Path to Tourist Stop. By Wayne Ludwig. (College Station: Texas A&M University Press, 2018. Pp. 368. Appendix, photographs, maps, notes, bibliography, index.) The cover art of Wayne Ludwig’s The Old Chisholm Trail: From Cow Path to Tourist Stop typifies the old-time cattle-driving life: a horse-mounted cowboy-driver looks back at a longhorn herd, distant hills, and white thunder-heads in brooding gray skies, evoking bygone cow-path days before major railhead destinations provided easterners’ beef and the drovers and trail bosses’ gold and later became major tourism markets. The legend of the cowboy fed tourists’ imaginations and opened a new revenue stream for Texas and other trail states. By the twenty-first century, the history of cattle trails needed facts more than legends. At a Chisholm Trail marker rededication in 2000, Ludwig, a native of Fort Worth, asked this serendipitous question, “Why is there a Chisholm Trail marker post in Fort Worth?” (xiii). The deep research he conducted to answer that question takes the reader to those facts; his purpose is to “avoid preconceived conclusions, seek the facts, follow the trail of evidence wherever it led, determine what can and cannot be corroborated by data . . . and let the chips fall where they may” (xiv). Ludwig’s book, the first in the Nancy and Ted Paup Ranching Heritage Series, shows his passion and skill for sifting through voluminous collections of lore, legend, fiction, and opinions presented as fact as he searches for documented evidence. The lyrics, “I’ll tell you my troubles on the Old Chisholm Trail,” become the theme for the book’s seventeen chapters and nine-page timeline, which stretches from 1493 to 1938. Ludwig’s major focus is the Chisholm Trail’s route and its many debated names, but he also includes other major cattle trails, which vastly increased his need for deep research. For example, he details Oklahoma oilman P. P. Ackley’s efforts to mark the Chisholm Trail in Texas and his controversial efforts to rename its sister trail to the west, Longhorn Chisholm, by placing monuments at Doan’s Crossing on the Red River. Later, Ackley linked the Meridian Highway project to the Chisholm Trail, a move supported by the U.S. Good Roads Association. Ludwig’s verification of trail names included “maps with provenance to a particular historical period” (172). He explains issues of fact using newspapers and books such as J. [End Page 127] Marvin Hunter’s The Trail Drivers of Texas (Cokesbury Press, 1925). Readers also learn that the names “Chisholm Trail” and “Great Western Trail” are pending as names for National Historic Trails. Even with the author’s exacting research, one especially significant fact remained elusive: the use of “Great” in the name of the Great Western Trail (the sister trail to the Chisholm Trail). Ludwig says, “Great Western Trail is currently popular but does not appear to be grounded in fact, as no reference that includes ‘Great’ as part of the name during the trail’s period of use is found” (115). He also says, “Accounts of the Chisholm Trail name in Texas cannot be verified against other data from 1867 to 1887 because such data do not seem to exist” (188). However, Ludwig overlooked two important sources. First, “Great Western Cattle Trail” is used during the trail period by John R. Cook in his memoir from 1877 to 1881, The Border and the Buffalo: An Untold Story of the Southwest Plains (Crane, 1907). The second is the definitive study, “Great Western Cattle Trail to Dodge City, Kansas,” a 1965 master’s thesis by Texas Tech history instructor and archivist Jimmy M. Skaggs. Ludwig’s otherwise impressive research results in nearly two hundred pages of text, fifty pages of notes, forty pages of maps, photos, and trail documents, and a thirty-page bibliography. His book now stands as a companion to the first comprehensive Chisholm Trail study, Wayne Gard’s The Chisholm Trail (University of Oklahoma Press, 1954). papers.title: Storied Ground: Landscape and the Shaping of English National Identity
papers.title_normalized: i storied ground landscape and the shaping of english national identity i
papers.abstract: In this insightful, original, and gracefully written analysis of six iconic English landscapes and their relationship to English (and occasionally British) national identity, Readman brings together art and history with great fluidity. As he points out, the value of landscapes often depends on factors other than their perceived physical properties. Nor do the sources of English identity in the nineteenth century—the focus of this book—lie solely in written histories, the evolution of the historical profession, or state-sponsored events such as world’s fairs. On the contrary, the places discussed in Storied Ground—the cliffs of Dover, the Northumbrian borderland, the Lake District, the New Forest, the city of Manchester, and the Thames River—show how landscapes helped to define the cultural boundaries of the nation, provided a sense of connection between past and present, and developed and deepened a sense of Englishness that was urban and rural, national and imperial, local and regional, and, most importantly, popular and democratic.Starting with the basic premises that all landscapes are human constructs and that all nations claim a homeland or bounded territory, Part I traces the process by which landscape was transformed into heritage. As with the American West and the Swiss Alps, the border landscapes that comprise the book’s first section—the Dover cliffs and the Northumbrian borderland—complicate English identity. The cliffs, which attracted little attention before the middle of the eighteenth century, became “powerful symbols of defense, defiance and difference,” eventually standing for “insular ideas of English nationhood” (26–27). Even as they marked Britain’s separateness from the European continent, they also represented home for weary travelers returning from overseas. More complicated was the Northumbrian borderland, a barren, bleak landscape that was rehabilitated not just in purely visual terms but also as an emblem of British national identity, even though its characteristic speech (the burr) gave it a distinctive regional identity.Part II deals with efforts to preserve the Lake District and the New Forest. In the late nineteenth century, just as the Lake District’s appeal as a tourist destination was widening, it became the focus of an emerging preservationist movement. But this change was not solely for the sake of aesthetics; the area came to be seen, in the words of William Wordsworth, as “national property” for people of all social classes who traveled there for rest and recreation at a time when the Third Reform Act of 1884/5 was producing a more democratic national identity. Readman argues that the National Trust’s campaign to purchase land in the Lake District was not animated by Tory paternalism so much as by popular patriotism. Meanwhile the New Forest lost its relevance as a crown game reserve and a source of timber for Britain’s navy, and came to be viewed instead as a “freely accessible historical landscape of liberty” (179). The Rufus Stone, which marked the spot where the unpopular King Rufus had been killed in 1100, and the ruins of Beaulieu Abbey, helped to link the forest to England’s medieval past as well.Part III, especially the chapter about Manchester, enriches the story even further. In every way the antithesis of rural England, the dark, dirty, dystopian “shock city” of the Industrial Revolution nonetheless became a popular tourist destination, its factories eliciting expressions of wonder and awe not least because they were seen to be doing “patriotic work” (206). Readman highlights the Italianate designs of its warehouses, which led to Manchester’s reputation as “the Florence…of the nineteenth century,” and the Gothic Revival public buildings, which combined “modernity and historicity” (231), preserving the past even as urban development was laying it to waste. The final chapter traces the Thames River’s growing association with commerce, culture, and the course of history as it meandered its way from rural Gloucestershire through London to the North Sea, connecting “countryside and capital, backwater and bustling port” (252), the national and the imperial. It became a matter of pride that the fine houses and country estates, which symbolized inherited wealth and beautified the riverside, could coexist, although not always comfortably, with mass tourism.No mere summary of this book can do it justice. The forty aptly chosen and carefully analyzed illustrations include engravings and photographs as well as oil paintings and even Punch cartoons. This book should be of great interest to historians and art historians, as well as those interested in tourism, historical preservation, and the construction of national identities. It is both scholarly and accessible, a model of interdisciplinary scholarship.

papers.title: Muse of Exit Ramps
papers.title_normalized: muse of exit ramps
papers.abstract: Muse of Exit Ramps Laura C. Stevenson (bio) Vermont Exit Ramps II Neil Shepard and Anthony Reczek Green Writers Press/Sundog Poetry Center www.greenwriterspress.com 124 Pages; Print, $24.95 One May morning some years ago, the Vermont poet Neil Shepard started at I-89’s Stowe/ Waterbury interchange and headed south, turning off the superhighway at every subsequent exit to observe its cloverleafs, bridges, and underpasses; his project was to “crystallize” his impressions of these “ramplands” into a few poems. The journey, which continued south to the Massachusetts border on I-91 after its intersection with I-89, took three days. The crystallizations took longer—perhaps becoming poetic rest areas as Shepard concentrated on the more extensive journeys of T(ravel)/ Unt(ravel) (2011)—but they eventually appeared in the chapbook Vermont Exit Ramps (2012). Vermont Exit Ramps II is a continuation of the project, which grew from a three-day lark to a five-year series of reflective trips along 381 Interstate miles. The new collection reprints thirteen of the original twenty-five poems and adds twenty-seven more; it covers all but the Burlington city exits north of Stowe (I-89) and White River Junction (I-91). The poems are enhanced by Anthony Reczek’s photographs of the ramplands’s fragile spring loveliness, and the collaboration, handsomely published by Brattleboro’s Green Writers Press, is a beautiful book. Readers familiar with Reczek’s style from his unobtrusively spectacular pictures in Vermont Life might expect Vermont Exit Ramps II to extend the image of an “unspoiled Vermont” that the magazine has promoted for seventy years. Be not deceived. The collection is, in Shepard’s words, “a book of post-pastoral poems,” and the couplets of its invocation, “Vermont Exits,” introduce a compromised Arcadia: Who will claim the kingdom of exit ramps and cloverleafs on the hillsides of I-89, these realms of birch and pine Rippling in mountain wind on a spring day, domains of quiet forgetfulness, places ravaged and recovered – Shepard and Reczek’s ramplands are beautiful precisely because they are un-cherished. No longer of interest to the ravaging forces of progress, have become demesnes “no one claims, the heavy machinery / having rattled past and gouged a pasture elsewhere.” Ostensibly, “I-89, Exit 10: Stowe/Waterbury” begins the sequence of exit poems because it’s the interchange closest to Shepard’s home in Johnson. Thematically, however, it portrays the face of post-pastoral Vermont by describing the geological and cultural metamorphosis brought about by the Interstates’ accommodation of Vermont’s ski industry. Exit 10’s rampland is “Blasted through fifty feet of granite / to make this exit ‘Vermont’/ for tourists.” Tourism, of course, preceded the Interstate; nineteenth-century visitors could see “the Summit / House built as the Civil War broke out,” or take “the Toll Road to the top of Mansfield / finished in 1870.” But “this history” began when Stowe’s residents innocently discovered skiing, thus opening the way to the literal and figurative Iron Age destruction of Vermont’s Arcadian foundations: This history has a moneyed glide, a schuss through powder, a hottub view and a gold club perched high on a hillside. Beneath it, loggers felling trees on a ski slope, road crews with sledgehammer, pickaxe, demolition dynamite. That dynamite exposed a prehistoric past, Granite before you thought of granite. Granite before the dynamite blast, before the tourist-idea: Best Western Café Grill, Blush Hill Country Club, Stowe Street Emporium. ATM. This is ravage and commercial “renewal” brought about by the worship of progress “that bedevils us in this late-capitalist culture.” The collection as a whole, however, is no diatribe; for the most part, it juxtaposes despoliation and beauty in the way earlier pastorals juxtaposed Court and Country. The “post-” in its pastoral lies in the witty irony with which the poems portray a “renewed” twenty-first century Vermont in which the Golden Age and the Iron Age share the same landscape. Sometimes the old and new parallel each other: at the end of the Middlesex exit (I-89 #9), for example, “turn right” and you’re headed to ski towns, but Turn left and meet Through Way Ends...

papers.title: IN MEMORY OF DR. OLEKSANDR KITSERA
papers.title_normalized: in memory of dr oleksandr kitsera
papers.authors: Andriy Bazylevych; Oleksandr Kitsera; Volodymyr Hayevskyy
papers.abstract: Oleksandr Omelianovych Kitsera was born on February 24, 1931, in the city of Lutsk, Volyn, into a family with deep Ukrainian and European traditions. His father, Omelian Kitsera, was an officer of the Ukrainian Galician Army, while his mother, Yulia Kitsera, worked as a secretary in Symon Petliura’s Directory. They met in Kamianets-Podilskyi during the hostilities. Later, the couple returned to Lviv, where they worked at the Audit Union of Ukrainian Cooperatives. In the 1930s, Omelian Kitsera organized the cooperative movement in Volyn, and it was there that their first child was born. Oleksandr Omelianovych remembered his mother with particular warmth. She had a literary talent: she wrote the libretto for the opera Zakhar Berkut, translated the works of Ivan Franko into Russian, created fairy tales and short stories for children, and left behind memoirs of her family's childhood. His father, meanwhile, had the privilege of serving as the personal attendant and bodyguard to Metropolitan Andrei Sheptytsky during the latter’s 1921 visit to the Ukrainian Academy of Economics in Poděbrady. It is symbolic that, years later, the Kitsers’ son also had a brief audience with Metropolitan Andrei before entering the first grade of the Private Coeducational School of Saint Josaphat in Lviv. The Metropolitan’s blessing became his spiritual guide throughout his life. Oleksandr Omelianovych received his education at the School of the Basilian Sisters in Lviv, the Ukrainian Academic Gymnasium, and Secondary School No. 1 in Lviv. In 1954, he graduated from the Faculty of Medicine of the Lviv State Medical Institute, having completed a one-year subinternship in otorhinolaryngology. He worked as an otolaryngologist in Liubeshiv, Volyn, later in Bibrka, Lviv Region, and at the United Military Hospital of the Border Troops. He completed a clinical residency and postgraduate studies, culminating in the successful defense of his Candidate of Medical Sciences dissertation in 1966, entitled The Role of Endoscopic Methods in the Diagnosis of Malignant Neoplasms of the Respiratory Tract. He developed techniques for bronchoscopy under general anesthesia and improved the application of endoscopic optics in clinical practice. From 1966 onward, his professional life was closely associated with the Department of Otorhinolaryngology of the Lviv Medical Institute (now the Danylo Halytsky Lviv National Medical University), where he served as an assistant professor, associate professor, professor, and, from 1981 to 2002, Head of the Department. In 1976, he defended his Doctor of Medical Sciences dissertation entitled Olfactory Disorders in Diseases of the Upper Respiratory Tract. Oleksandr Omelianovych’s scientific interests encompassed rhinology and olfactology, reconstructive surgery of the nose and paranasal sinuses, ENT oncology, the inhalational use of mineral waters, the application of lasers in otorhinolaryngology, interdisciplinary issues at the interface of endocrinology and otorhinolaryngology, the selection of grafts for rhinological surgery, as well as the history of medicine, bioethics, and medical deontology. Oleksandr Kitsera published more than 400 scientific papers and was the author or co-author of numerous textbooks, manuals, and clinical guides on the propedeutics and clinical practice of otorhinolaryngology, including emergency otorhinolaryngology. He was the holder of eight inventor’s certificates and more than twenty certificates for rationalization proposals. An important area of his work was medical terminology. He compiled the otorhinolaryngology section of the Orthographic Dictionary of Ukrainian Medical Terms and participated in the preparation of the two-volume Ukrainian–Latin–English Explanatory Medical Dictionary, the four-volume Ukrainian–Latin–English Medical Encyclopedic Dictionary, and the seven-language Lexicon of the Otorhinolaryngologist. Oleksandr Omelianovych authored and published the following textbooks and manuals: Endoscopy of the Respiratory Tract and Esophagus (methodological recommendations, 1976); Practicum in Otolaryngology (manual, 1981); Lectures on Otolaryngology (manual, 1991–1995); Propedeutics of Otorhinolaryngology (manual, co-authored, 1993); Clinical Otorhinolaryngology (textbook, co-authored with members of the Department of Otorhinolaryngology, 1996); Medications in Otorhinolaryngology (textbook, co-authored, 1999); Clinical Otorhinolaryngology (textbook, co-authored with members of the Department of Otorhinolaryngology, 2006); Tinnitus (manual, co-authored with D. I. Zabolotnyi and O. O. Kitsera, 2009); Lectures on Otolaryngology (multimedia manual, 2015); The Nasal Mucosa (Clinical Morphology, Physiology, Pathology, and Pharmacology) (co-authored with V. V. Chopyak and O. O. Kitsera, 2016); Orthorhinia (manual for physicians, 2017); Propedeutics of Otorhinolaryngology (textbook for medical interns and participants in postgraduate medical education, co-authored with members of the Department of Otorhinolaryngology, 2019); Emergency Otorhinolaryngology in Peacetime and Wartime (manual for medical interns and participants in postgraduate medical education, co-authored with members of the Department of Otorhinolaryngology, 2020). During the last years of his life, he focused on autoimmune diseases and syndromes in the practice of otorhinolaryngology. He had nearly completed a new textbook, Clinical Otorhinolaryngology, which he did not live to publish. During the 1980s, he actively promoted international scientific cooperation, particularly by coordinating academic collaboration with the Medical Academy in Białystok, Poland. The early 1990s marked a period of particularly intense public engagement. From 1991 to 1993, he served as President of the Ukrainian Medical Society in Lviv and was one of the initiators of its revival in independent Ukraine. He was a co-founder of the Marian Panchyshyn Museum of the History of Galician Medicine and contributed to preserving the memory of Galicia’s distinguished physicians. In 1991–1992, he served as editor of and regular contributor to the medical newspaper Narodne Zdorovia (People’s Health), promoting medical knowledge among a broad readership. From 1995, he was a full member of the Shevchenko Scientific Society. He participated in the revival of the Society, was actively involved in the Prosvita Society for the Ukrainian Language and the People's Hospital, and initiated the restoration of the Sich Riflemen's graves. He also took part in the founding assembly of the People's Movement of Ukraine (Rukh) and contributed to numerous civic initiatives supporting Ukrainian science and culture. He received numerous honors and awards, including the Metropolitan Andrei Sheptytsky Medal "For the Revival of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church," the Yevhen Ozarkevych Medal, Certificates of Honor from the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine and the Ministry of Health of Ukraine, the honorary distinction "Distinguished Service to Danylo Halytsky Lviv National Medical University," the "Golden Coat of Arms of Lviv" award, and many other Ukrainian and international distinctions. Beyond medicine, he was an enthusiastic traveler and outdoor enthusiast. He undertook mountain expeditions of varying levels of difficulty in the Carpathians, the Caucasus, and the Altai Mountains, participated in kayaking trips along Ukrainian rivers and the rivers and lakes of Karelia, and explored the caves of the Ternopil region. He held sports tourism qualifications, served for a time as President of the Lviv Regional Sports Tourism Club, and organized the first mass ascents of Mount Hoverla ("Hoverliany"). He also enjoyed woodworking and caring for the garden surrounding his home. Alongside his medical career, he was deeply engaged in literary work. He wrote short stories, novellas, and essays and translated from Polish, German, and English. His published books include At the Crossroads of Life, Laughter and Sin, Pilgrimage, Knights of the Pen and the Scalpel, The Ukrainian Paths of Ivan Mikulicz, and The Bright Weapon of Yurii Lypa. He also worked extensively on the history of medicine and prominent figures of Ukrainian culture, preparing the monograph They Treated the Ukrainian Shakespeare: Physicians in the Life of Lesya Ukrainka. Shortly before his death, he completed an autobiographical book for publication. Even during the COVID-19 pandemic, he remained actively engaged in teaching, introducing distance learning lectures and preparing Illustrated Clinical Cases in Otorhinolaryngology for publication. Throughout his life, Oleksandr Omelianovych remained a man of profound faith, integrity, and high moral culture. He deeply loved his family and was a devoted father and grandfather, taking particular joy in his two grandsons, to whom he passed on his love of knowledge, the Ukrainian language, and his profession. For many generations of students, he became not only a teacher of medicine but also a moral role model. Oleksandr Omelianovych Kitsera passed away on February 18, 2026, just a few days before his ninety-fifth birthday. He was laid to rest in the cemetery of the city of Sambir beside his beloved wife, Oksana. His life stands as an enduring example of wholehearted service to medicine, Ukrainian science, culture, and society. The memory of Professor Kitsera — as a physician, scholar, teacher, and devoted citizen — will live on through his scientific legacy, his students, and the countless good works that have left a lasting mark on the history of Ukrainian medicine.
